docs.title: Parakeet
docs.text:
A data-parallel compiler for numerical Python.

Write ordinary NumPy, loops, comprehensions, or explicit data-parallel operators (map, reduce, scan, allpairs). Parakeet specializes your function for its input types, fuses and tiles the array algebra, and compiles native code for multi-core CPUs, Apple Metal, and NVIDIA CUDA.

Get started Explore the gallery

docs.title: Exact nearest neighbor
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import parakeet as par


@par.jit
def nearest(x, y):
  delta = x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]
  d2 = np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2)
  return np.argmin(d2, axis=1)

Parakeet computes distances a tile at a time on both CPU and GPU, keeping only the winning reference index per tile rather than allocating the full N × M distance matrix. Ties preserve NumPy's first-index rule.

Compare timings, scaling, and memory

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
python -m pip install parakeet

Requires Python 3.11+, NumPy 2, and a system C compiler. For GPU backends, install parakeet[metal] on Apple Silicon or parakeet[cuda12] with an NVIDIA GPU.

docs.title: One algebra underneath
docs.text:
Most numerical Python (NumPy expressions, comprehensions, or explicit parallel operators) expresses the same handful of array computations: maps, reductions, scans, filters, and scatters.

@par.jit
def scaled_tanh_numpy(x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.3):
  return np.tanh(x * alpha) + beta


@par.jit
def scaled_tanh_comp(x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.3):
  return np.array([np.tanh(xi * alpha) + beta for xi in x])

Both lower to the same single fused parallel loop with no temporary arrays. Keeping that operator algebra intact through the middle end lets a small set of general passes do the heavy lifting:

  • Fusion. Chained array expressions, filtered reductions (np.sum(x[x > 0])), and sibling histograms sharing the same bin IDs merge into one pass. See the tree-split example.
  • Tiling and single-pass reductions. Associative reductions and bilinear products tile into cache or GPU shared memory, so Gaussian kernel regression, nearest-neighbor search, and attention stream blocks instead of allocating giant pairwise matrices. Read the algebraic laws.
  • Gradients. parakeet.grad and parakeet.value_and_grad differentiate the array operators directly, compiling a training step into one native function. Learn about gradients.
  • Inspection. Every stage is visible: inspect the operator IR, see which rewrites fired with parakeet.show_rewrite, or read the generated C, Metal, or CUDA source. Inspect a rewrite.

docs.title: Algebraic laws
docs.text:
Parakeet lowers numerical Python to a small algebra of data-parallel operators (maps, reductions, scans, and filters) with fusion and tiling rules over them. Those rules eliminate temporary arrays and improve cache locality for ordinary array expressions, comprehensions, and matrix products.

Many modern numerical and machine-learning kernels need one step further: eliminating quadratic O(N²) or O(M · V) intermediates, turning long serial recurrences into parallel block passes, and avoiding saving giant intermediates for reverse-mode differentiation. Rather than adding special-purpose "layer" ops to the compiler, Parakeet encodes these transformations as six general algebraic laws over a small core of index-operator statements (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, IndexExpand, IndexScatter, IndexWavefront, and IndexTile / TileStage) plus multi-state Carry folds.

Because the passes match operator algebra instead of model names, the same rules fire on Gaussian kernel regression, shortest-path products, exact nearest-neighbor search, histogram split-finding, and IIR filters as on attention, cross-entropy, and state-space models.

docs.title: Semantic contract: real-algebraic rewrites vs. exact order
docs.text:
Algebraic rewrites (parallel reduction, monoidal tiling, contraction reassociation, chunkwise affine scans, privatized scatter-add) rely on real-arithmetic associativity and commutativity: floating-point rounding order may differ in the last ULP relative to a left-to-right loop, just as in NumPy's pairwise summation or cuBLAS. That assumption is explicit and deliberate in Parakeet.

Where order is semantically observable; equal-distance ties and first-NaN propagation in argmin / argmax, non-commutative structured parakeet.fold merges, or general sequential reductions; Parakeet preserves exact left-to-right merge order across chunks and tiles (and refuses to parallelize non-associative combiners).

docs.title: The six laws at a glance
docs.text: Law Algebraic idea Middle-end pass Example workloads Law 1: Rescaled semiring monoids Associative rescaling fold (m₁, l₁, o₁) ⊕ (m₂, l₂, o₂) monoidal tiling Softmax attention, Split-K decoding, linear cross-entropy, Gaussian (RBF) kernel regression, 1-pass logsumexp Law 2: Algebraic AD rematerialization Sufficient-statistic VJPs that recompute score tiles on the fly algebraic_vjp (in autodiff) Attention backward (no N × N saved), cross-entropy backward (no M × V saved), 1-pass LayerNorm / RMSNorm VJP Law 3: Bilinear contraction reassociation & shared-KV tiling (U @ Vᵀ) @ Wᵀ = U @ (Vᵀ @ Wᵀ) + folding shared-KV query groups into tiles contraction reassociation Multi-head latent attention absorption, grouped-query attention, low-rank (X @ A) @ B chains Law 4: Chunkwise state-space duality Affine composition (a₂, b₂) ∘ (a₁, b₁) = (a₂ a₁, a₂ b₁ + b₂) and block duality chunkwise scan Parallel IIR / EMA / Kalman filters, Mamba-2 and gated linear attention recurrences Law 5: Affine tile-interval pruning Interval bounds [i₀, i₀+Bₘ-1] × [j₀, j₀+Bₙ-1] over index predicates TileInterval in analysis Causal and sliding-window masks, banded matrices, spatial cutoffs, runtime boolean tile skipping Law 6: Privatized scatter & multi-state carries Commutative/associative scatter-add and ordered multi-field folds IndexScatter, Fold.carries, pairwise fold tiling GBDT histogram splits, exact 1-NN search, argmin/argmax with values, sparse updates

docs.title: Law 1: Rescaled semiring monoids
docs.text:
Any reduction whose output depends on a global normalizing statistic (a row maximum m, a sum of exponentials l, or a norm) can fuse with a downstream weighted sum in a single tiled pass whenever its running state forms an associative monoid (S, ⊕, e).

For softmax-weighted contractions (attention and Gaussian kernel regression), the state carries the running maximum m, normalizing sum l, and unnormalized output vector o:

m = max(m₁, m₂)
(m₁, l₁, o₁) ⊕ (m₂, l₂, o₂) = (
    m,
    l₁ · exp(m₁ - m) + l₂ · exp(m₂ - m),
    o₁ · exp(m₁ - m) + o₂ · exp(m₂ - m),
)

Because ⊕ is associative, the same monoid covers four workloads without allocating an N × M or M × V matrix:

  1. Tiled softmax attention (flash_monoid): streams tiles of K and V through CPU cache or GPU shared memory against a tile of Q, never materializing the score matrix S or probability matrix P.
  2. Split-K decoding (split_k=True): when the query grid is too small to fill a GPU (for instance, autoregressive decode with small T_q and long T_kv), Parakeet splits T_kv across threadblocks computing partial (mₚ, lₚ, oₚ) summaries and merges them with the same ⊕.
  3. Tiled linear cross-entropy (monoid_lse): tiles H @ W over the vocabulary dimension V using the scalar (m, l) monoid while gathering the target score on the fly, avoiding an M × V logit matrix.
  4. Gaussian / RBF kernel regression (score_op="sqdist"): recognizes -γ · ||xᵢ - yⱼ||² feeding a normalized exponential sum and compiles Nadaraya-Watson smoothing into one O(N + M)-memory kernel.

docs.title: Law 2: Algebraic rematerialization in reverse-mode AD
docs.text:
A naive reverse-mode tape saves every forward intermediate, which would bring back O(N²) memory for attention and O(M · V) memory for linear cross-entropy. Parakeet's tape optimizer (parakeet/transforms/algebraic_vjp.py) runs at the operator level before lowering and substitutes sufficient-statistic adjoints where an algebraic identity exists:

  • Attention backward (flash_monoid_bwd): saves only (Q, K, V, O, lse): no N × N tensor is kept. A cheap O(N · D) pass computes Dᵢ = sum_d dO[i, d] · O[i, d], and the tiled backward kernel recomputes each score tile P = exp(S - lse) and dS = P · (dO @ Vᵀ - D) in on-chip memory while accumulating dK and dV.
  • Linear cross-entropy backward (cce_bwd): saves only (H, W, targets, lse) and recomputes tile probabilities p[i, v] = exp(hᵢ · wᵥ - lseᵢ) while accumulating dH and dW.
  • LayerNorm and RMSNorm VJP: collapses multi-pass mean/variance backward graphs into a single pass over the saved normalized output and inverse scale.
  • Standalone softmax VJP: drops the max adjoint completely using dS = P · (dP - sum(P · dP)).

docs.title: Law 3: Bilinear contraction reassociation & shared-KV tiling
docs.text:
For a chain of two bilinear contractions sharing a single-use intermediate T:

T[u, k] = sum_r U[u, r] · V[k, r]
Y[p, u] = sum_k W[p, k] · T[u, k]

reassociating the summation order computes the same result:

M[p, r] = sum_k W[p, k] · V[k, r]
Y[p, u] = sum_r M[p, r] · U[u, r]

parakeet/transforms/reassociate.py compares the multiply-add counts U·K·(R + P) against P·R·(K + U) and chooses the cheaper order:

  • Latent attention absorption: given K = C_kv @ W_uk, V = C_kv @ W_uv, and O = softmax(Q @ Kᵀ) @ V, Law 3 emits a runtime shape-guarded branch that absorbs W_uk into Q (Q_abs = Q @ W_ukᵀ) and moves W_uv after attention (O = (P @ C_kv) @ W_uv). Because monoidal tiling (Law 1) runs right after Law 3 on both branches, short-query decode runs tiled attention directly over the compressed latent C_kv without materializing expanded K or V, while long-query prefill automatically takes the lower-FLOP expanded branch.
  • Low-rank matrix chains: (X @ A) @ B and X @ (A @ B) pick the lower-FLOP association at runtime, and remain differentiable under grad.
  • Shared-KV head-group tiling: when a batch axis g of Q (size G) does not vary in K or V (grouped-query attention), Parakeet folds g into the query row index (i_eff = g * T_q + i) so all G query heads share one shared-memory load of K and V.

docs.title: Law 4: Chunkwise state-space duality
docs.text:
A sequential loop of length T has O(T) serial depth and cannot use multiple cores or GPU threadblocks directly. parakeet/transforms/tile_scan.py recognizes two associative recurrence patterns inside plain Python for t in range(T): loops:

  1. Affine recurrences (s[t] = a[t] * s[t - 1] + b[t]): covers exponential moving averages, IIR filters, and scalar Kalman filters. The loop is rewritten into a 3-stage chunkwise scan (chunk size C = 64) using affine composition (a₂, b₂) ∘ (a₁, b₁) = (a₂ a₁, a₂ b₁ + b₂), reducing serial depth by 64× with no O(T) temporary arrays.
  2. Bilinear matrix-state recurrences: 
    for t in range(T):
  S = a[t] * S + k[t][:, None] * v[t][None, :]
  out[t] = q[t] @ S
    Rewritten into a 4-step division-free chunkwise scan (C = 64):
  3. Step 0: parallel cumulative decay products inside each chunk (exact even when a[t] == 0 or a[t] < 0, and when T is not a multiple of C).
  4. Step 1: intra-chunk quadratic attention-form products Y_intra[c] = ((Q[c] @ K[c]ᵀ) * L[c]) @ V[c].
  5. Step 2: chunk state summary B[c] = K_scaled[c]ᵀ @ V[c].
  6. Step 3: 64× shorter inter-chunk recurrence S_in[c + 1] = A[c] * S_in[c] + B[c].
  7. Step 4: off-diagonal readout Y_off[c] = Q[c] @ S_in[c] combined with Y_intra[c].

Because chunkwise scan runs before tiling, the matrix products in Steps 1, 2, and 4 automatically flow into CPU register tiling, Metal simdgroup_matrix, and CUDA nvcuda::wmma Tensor Cores.

docs.title: Law 5: Affine tile-interval mask pruning
docs.text:
In parakeet/transforms/analysis.py, TileInterval propagates coordinate bounds [i₀, i₀ + B_M - 1] and [j₀, j₀ + B_N - 1] through affine index expressions and boolean connectives:

  • Causal masks (j <= i): proves tiles with j₀ > i₀ + B_M - 1 are entirely false (skipped before loading K or V) and tiles with j₀ + B_N - 1 <= i₀ are entirely true (run through a branchless inner loop).
  • Sliding windows ((j <= i) & (i - j <= W)): skips both future tiles and tiles outside the window, reducing O(N²) work to O(N · W) from ordinary mask code.
  • Runtime boolean masks: when a mask comes from a runtime array, GPU kernels cooperatively check whether any entry in the tile is true and skip empty tiles before loading values.

docs.title: Law 6: Privatized scatter & multi-state carries
docs.text:
Two patterns show up constantly outside dense linear algebra: accumulating into shared bins (np.bincount, parakeet.scatter_add) and folding structured state (argmin, Welford variance, custom parakeet.fold).

  • Keyed histogram fusion: sibling IndexScatter statements sharing the same index expression (such as gradient and Hessian histograms in a decision tree split search) merge into one traversal over the data, lowered with thread-privatized bins on CPU and parallel atomics/privatization on GPU.
  • Ordered multi-state carries and pairwise tile folds: Fold.carries tracks multiple scalar accumulators in one reduction pass while preserving chunk order (so leftmost ties in argmin or non-commutative compositions in parakeet.fold stay exact). pairwise fold tiling fuses a pairwise score producer directly into an ordered fold over bounded tiles on both CPU and GPU; eliminating the full N × M distance matrix in both broadcasting NumPy and nested-map 1-NN.

docs.title: Inspecting rewrites with parakeet.show_rewrite
docs.text:
Call parakeet.show_rewrite on any function to see which laws fired, which tiled plans were selected, and the operator IR before and after the middle-end passes:

import numpy as np
import parakeet as par


@par.jit
def causal_attention(q, k, v):
  causal = par.imap(lambda i, j: i >= j, (q.shape[0], k.shape[0]))
  s = np.where(causal, (q @ k.T) * np.float32(0.125), np.float32(-1e9))
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ v


q = np.zeros((128, 64), np.float32)
print(par.show_rewrite(causal_attention, q, q, q).summary())

Parakeet Algebraic Rewrite Report for `causal_attention`
  Laws triggered : Law 1: Rescaled Semiring Monoid Tile Fusion, Law 5: Affine Tile-Interval Mask Pruning
  Monoidal plans : flash_monoid
  Operators      : IndexMap 5 -> 1 | IndexTile 1 | IndexScatter 0 -> 0 | Carry folds 0

See the Kernel gallery for runnable examples and timings across all six laws.

docs.title: parakeet.jit
docs.text:
Compile a numerical Python function to native code on first call.

Use it bare (@jit) or with options (@jit(backend="metal")). The function is specialised for each distinct combination of argument types; every later call with the same types runs the cached native code.

Options (all default to the corresponding parakeet.config setting):

backend "auto", "c", "multicore", "threads", "openmp", "gcd", "metal"/"mps", "cuda" or "python". bounds_check Raise IndexError for out-of-range indices instead of crashing. fusion Fuse array expressions into single loops. tiling Tile matmul-shaped loops for cache locality.

docs.title: parakeet.grad(f, argnum=0)
docs.text:
The gradient of the scalar-valued function f with respect to its argument number argnum (or, for a tuple, to each of those arguments).

grad(f)(*args) takes the arguments of f and returns an array shaped like the differentiated argument (a tuple of arrays for a tuple of argument numbers; nested tuples of parameters give nested tuples of gradients). Works inside compiled code and from plain Python.

docs.title: parakeet.value_and_grad(f, argnum=0)
docs.text: Like :func:grad, but the new function returns (f(*args), gradient).

docs.title: parakeet.jvp(fn, primals, tangents)
docs.text:
Forward-mode Jacobian-vector product: returns (fn(*primals), d_fn).

primals and tangents are tuples of arguments matching fn (or single values for unary functions). Works from plain Python and inside @par.jit or other AD transforms with zero tape and O(1) extra memory.

docs.title: parakeet.vjp(fn, *primals)
docs.text:
General non-scalar reverse-mode AD: returns (primal_out, vjp_fn).

vjp_fn(cotangent) returns a tuple of input cotangents matching primals for arbitrary scalar, array, tuple, record, or RaggedArray outputs.

docs.title: parakeet.linearize(fn, *primals)
docs.text: Linearize fn at primals: returns (primal_out, lin_fn) where lin_fn(*tangents) computes the directional derivative JVP(fn, primals, tangents).

docs.title: parakeet.linear_transpose(linear_fn, *example_inputs)
docs.text: Return transpose_fn(cotangent) computing L^T(cotangent) for a linear function L.

docs.text:

Runs in ~2x reverse-mode cost with zero O(N^2) Hessian allocation.

docs.title: parakeet.DeviceArray
docs.text:
An array resident on a GPU device (Metal or CUDA) across @jit calls.

Created with :func:parakeet.to_device or returned automatically by a @jit function called with DeviceArray inputs. Passing a DeviceArray into subsequent @jit calls on the same device avoids redundant host-to-device uploads, and GPU-computed outputs are promoted directly to DeviceArray without device-to-host downloads — keeping weights, gradients, and optimizer state resident on the GPU throughout a training loop.

Call :meth:numpy or :func:parakeet.to_host (or np.asarray(da)) to bring the contents back to host memory.

docs.title: parakeet.seed(value=None)
docs.text:
Seed the random number generator used by np.random in compiled code.

Compiled code has its own counter-based generator (it must be usable from many threads and on GPUs), so streams differ from NumPy's, but are reproducible for a given seed and sequence of calls.

docs.title: parakeet.show_rewrite(fn, *args, backend=None, blas=False, **opts)
docs.text:
Compile-only algebraic rewrite inspection for fn on the types of args.

Works reliably on cold or warm specializations (including repeated calls and calls after ordinary execution), supports plain functions, @parakeet.jit functions, and grad / value_and_grad wrappers without executing fn or mutating global compiler state.

docs.title: parakeet.fold(el, lift, merge, x, init=None, *, axis=None, indexed=False, emit=None)
docs.text:
Lift elements to scalar/fixed-vector tuple states and merge adjacent states in input order.

With no axis, lift each leading slice and return one state. With an axis, fold the lanes along that axis and project each state with emit (which may return a scalar, a fixed-size array, or a tuple/NamedTuple of them). An indexed lift receives (value, index) with the index local to its lane. A supplied seed is applied once on the left; an unseeded empty fold raises.

docs.title: parakeet.find_broken_transform(fn, inputs, expected=None, print_transforms=True, print_functions=True)
docs.text:
Name of the first optimization that makes fn(*inputs) differ from expected (by default: what the function returns when run by Python).

Returns None if the compiled function is right with everything on, and "frontend" if it is already wrong with every optimization off.

docs.title: parakeet.verify(fn, phase='')
docs.text:
Verify structural, scoping, typing, and ownership invariants of fn.

Returns fn so it can be used inline; raises :class:InternalError on any violation.

docs.title: parakeet.errors
docs.text:
Exception hierarchy.

Compile-time problems are reported as :class:CompileError subclasses that carry the location of the offending Python source, so the message points at the user's code rather than at Parakeet internals. Runtime problems detected by generated code (out-of-bounds indices, shape mismatches, ...) are re-raised as the same built-in exception NumPy/Python would have raised.

docs.title: Automatic differentiation
docs.text:
Parakeet provides composable reverse-mode, forward-mode, and higher-order automatic differentiation directly over its operator IR. Every differentiated function compiles into ordinary fused, tiled, parallel CPU or GPU loops alongside the rest of your program:

API What it computes par.grad(f, argnum=0) Reverse-mode gradient of a scalar-valued function par.value_and_grad(f, argnum=0) Forward value and reverse-mode gradient in one compiled call par.jvp(f, primals, tangents) Forward-mode Jacobian-vector product (f(*primals), J_f(*primals) · tangents) par.vjp(f, *primals) General non-scalar reverse-mode (y, pullback) for array, tuple, record, or RaggedArray outputs par.linearize(f, *primals) Forward value y plus reusable linear JVP function t -> J_f(x) · t par.linear_transpose(f, *primals) Exact linear transpose u -> Lᵀ(u) of a linear function L par.hvp(f, primals, tangents) Forward-over-reverse Hessian-vector product ∇²f(x) · v par.jacfwd(f, argnum=0) / par.jacrev(f, argnum=0) Full Jacobian matrix via forward-mode or reverse-mode AD par.hessian(f, argnum=0) Full Hessian matrix via forward-over-reverse AD par.stop_gradient(x) Zero-copy gradient & tangent barrier @par.checkpoint Rematerialize a block's intermediates during backpropagation @par.custom_vjp / @par.custom_jvp Attach user-defined reverse-mode or forward-mode derivative rules

docs.title: Reverse-mode gradients (grad and value_and_grad)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import parakeet as par


def loss(w, x, y):
  return np.mean((np.tanh(x @ w) - y) ** 2)


g = par.grad(loss)(w, x, y)  # d loss / d w, shaped like w
value, g = par.value_and_grad(loss)(w, x, y)
gw, gx = par.grad(loss, (0, 1))(w, x, y)  # several arguments at once

For par.grad and par.value_and_grad, the function returns a single floating-point scalar. Differentiated arguments may be floats, float arrays, RaggedArrays, or arbitrarily nested tuples, NamedTuples, dicts, and frozen @dataclass records (discrete metadata fields such as int, bool, or str pass through cleanly as zero-tangent static leaves):

def mlp(params, x, y):
  (w1, b1), (w2, b2) = params
  h = np.tanh(x @ w1 + b1)
  return np.mean((h @ w2 + b2 - y) ** 2)


(gw1, gb1), (gw2, gb2) = par.grad(mlp)(params, x, y)

par.grad(f) can be called from plain Python, where it compiles on first use, or inside a @par.jit function, where the entire training step becomes one compiled function:

@par.jit
def descend(w, x, y, rate, steps):
  for _ in range(steps):
    w = w - rate * par.grad(loss)(w, x, y)
  return w

examples/nanogpt.py trains a small transformer this way, and examples/convnet.py trains a convolutional network.

docs.title: Forward-mode AD, general VJPs, and linear transposes
docs.text:
Use par.jvp for directional derivatives in a single forward pass (no backward tape, O(1) extra memory even through long for/while loops), and par.vjp when differentiating functions with vector, matrix, tuple, record, or RaggedArray outputs:

def f(x, w):
  z = np.tanh(x @ w)
  return z, np.sum(z * z, axis=1)


# Forward-mode directional derivative (JVP)
(y1, y2), (dy1, dy2) = par.jvp(f, (x, w), (vx, vw))

# General non-scalar reverse-mode pullback (VJP)
(y1, y2), pullback = par.vjp(f, x, w)
gx, gw = pullback((u1, u2))

For any differentiable function f, the transpose identity ⟨jvp(f, x, v), u⟩ == ⟨v, vjp(f, x)(u)⟩ holds to machine precision. par.linearize(f, *primals) returns (y, lin_fn) for repeated JVP evaluation at a point, and par.linear_transpose(L, *example_inputs) constructs the exact adjoint Lᵀ of a linear operator.

docs.title: Higher-order derivatives, HVPs, and Jacobians
docs.text:
par.hvp computes Hessian-vector products via forward-over-reverse AD (jvp(grad(f))) in one fused pass; including through checkpointed loops, LayerNorm, and zero-$O(T^2)$ rematerialized attention:

def objective(w, x):
  h = np.tanh(x @ w)
  return np.sum(h * h * h)


hv = par.hvp(lambda w_: objective(w_, x), w, v)  # ∇²f(w) · v (forward-over-reverse)
H = par.hessian(lambda w_: objective(w_, x))(w)  # full Hessian matrix
J_fwd = par.jacfwd(lambda w_: np.tanh(x @ w_))(w)  # forward-mode Jacobian
J_rev = par.jacrev(lambda w_: np.tanh(x @ w_))(w)  # reverse-mode Jacobian

Nested reverse-over-reverse par.grad(par.grad(...)) also works through element-wise operations, reductions, matrix products, views, np.stack / np.concatenate, np.cumsum, gather indexing (x[idx]), scatter-add (np.add.at, par.scatter_add), and scalar 1-to-1 par.map:

def penalty(w, x):
  g = par.grad(loss)(w, x)
  return np.sum(g * g)


par.grad(penalty)(w, x)  # 2 H g, reverse over reverse

docs.title: What can be differentiated
docs.text:
Category Supported operations Arithmetic and math + - * / **, np.exp, np.tanh, np.maximum, np.where, np.abs, np.clip, … with broadcasting Reductions np.sum, np.mean, np.var, np.std, np.max, np.min, np.prod (zero-safe), np.linalg.norm with axis/keepdims; par.reduce with np.add, np.multiply, np.minimum, np.maximum, or arbitrary user folds Linear algebra @, np.dot, np.matmul for vectors, matrices, and batches; np.einsum Scans, sorting, and selection np.cumsum, par.scan, np.sort, par.topk, par.topk_fold Indexing, lookup, and scatter Views (slice, T, reshape, ravel, np.transpose), gather x[idx], FrozenHashTable.get, SortedIndex.get, np.add.at, canonical for-loop out[idx[i]] += val[i], par.scatter_add Building arrays np.concatenate, np.stack, np.array([a, b, c]), comprehensions Parallel operators par.map / par.each, par.allpairs, par.imap, par.fold, par.wavefront / par.soft_align Structured types Nested tuples, NamedTuple, fixed string-key dicts, frozen @dataclass, RaggedArray

Derivatives of min, max, abs, and topk at a tie follow standard conventions: ties share the derivative equally.

docs.title: Loops and branches
docs.text:
Parakeet differentiates both small static loops and arbitrary runtime-bound for and while loops in forward and reverse mode:

  • Small static for loops (compile-time trip count <= 32 or iterating over a heterogeneous tuple of weight matrices) are unrolled onto the tape for zero checkpoint overhead and cross-iteration fusion.
  • Runtime-bound and long for loops (for t in range(n):, for x in arr:, or static ranges longer than 32 iterations; including 10,000+ iterations) compile to an IR-level O(sqrt(T)) checkpointed reverse loop (ForRange) with constant IR size and bounded memory.
  • Data-dependent while loops (while err > tol:) compile to a fixed-slot stride-doubling checkpointed reverse While loop (O(log T) slots, zero dynamic reallocation inside the loop).
  • Custom par.reduce folds use O(sqrt(N)) checkpointed reverse mode, and 1-D par.scan with any user combiner is differentiable directly.
  • Forward-mode par.jvp propagates tangents alongside the loop in a single forward pass with O(1) extra memory.
def deep(weights, x):  # a tuple of matrices (unrolled)
  for w in weights:
    x = np.tanh(x @ w)
  return np.sum(x)


def iir_loss(a, b, s0):  # runtime-length recurrence (O(sqrt(T)) checkpointed reverse loop)
  s = s0
  for t in range(a.shape[0]):
    s = a[t] * s + b[t]
  return s * s

Loops that do not touch differentiated values are left alone, so a training loop around par.grad is an ordinary loop. Loops containing break, continue, or early return over differentiated state are refused loudly.

An if statement whose condition is only known at run time is differentiated in reverse mode by running both branches and selecting between their results (like np.where). Branches touching differentiated values may only assign variables: no return, raise, break, or array stores. A guard that only raises (if n == 0: raise ValueError(...)) is allowed without running both sides.

docs.title: Custom rules, stop_gradient, and checkpoint
docs.text:
• par.stop_gradient(x) detaches a scalar, array, tuple, record, or RaggedArray from both reverse-mode grad/vjp and forward-mode jvp with zero copy: 
    y = x + par.stop_gradient(np.round(x) - x)
  • @par.custom_vjp attaches custom (fwd, bwd) rules via .defvjp(fwd, bwd): supporting NamedTuple, frozen @dataclass, and RaggedArray residuals, higher-order AD, and Implicit Function Theorem differentiation through while-loop equilibrium solvers without storing iteration history.
  • @par.custom_jvp attaches custom forward-mode rules via .defjvp(jvp_rule): 
    @par.custom_jvp
def smooth_relu(x):
  return np.maximum(x, 0.0)


@smooth_relu.defjvp
def _smooth_relu_jvp(primals, tangents):
  (x,) = primals
  (dx,) = tangents
  return np.maximum(x, 0.0), dx / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))
  • @par.checkpoint (or par.checkpoint(fn)(*args)) drops a block's forward intermediates and rematerializes them during backpropagation, composing cleanly with Parakeet's algebraic rematerialization rules for attention, linear cross-entropy, softmax, and LayerNorm / RMSNorm.

docs.title: Writing into arrays
docs.text:
Stores are differentiated: assigning a slice, an element, or updating in place (out[i] += v, np.add.at(out, idx, vals)) all work cleanly:

out = np.zeros((n, 3))
out[:3] = x[:3] @ w
out[3:] = np.tanh(x[3:] @ w)
out += bias

Going backwards, whatever adjoint arrived for the stored region belongs to the value that was stored, and the region starts again from zero. Overwriting a value that an earlier operation's derivative still has to read (y = np.tanh(h); h[0] = 5.0) is refused loudly, because the derivative of tanh needs the original h.

docs.title: The gradient is right or there is none
docs.text:
Parakeet never returns a derivative that silently drops part of your function. If something on the path from inputs to output lacks a derivative rule; such as np.cumprod, np.convolve, or an arbitrary indexed overwrite out[idx] = v; you get an UnsupportedError naming it:

UnsupportedError: cannot differentiate through cumprod() (line 12): its derivative is not implemented

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
While a function is elaborated, reverse-mode AD records each array operator on an algebraic tape (and forward-mode AD propagates symbolic tangents alongside primals). Because rules operate at the index-operator level before lowering:

  • Element-wise operators differentiate symbolically via partial derivatives.
  • parakeet/transforms/algebraic_vjp.py runs a composable registry of algebraic rematerialization rules (ALGEBRAIC_AD_RULES) for FlashAttention (VJP, JVP, and HVP with zero $O(T^2)$ allocations), linear cross-entropy, softmax, and LayerNorm / RMSNorm; both at top level and inside checkpointed loops.
  • Scalars and views are not recorded on the tape: scalar adjoints push straight down the expression tree, and a view of an array is the same view of its adjoint.

See parakeet/transforms/autodiff.py, parakeet/transforms/jvp.py, and parakeet/transforms/algebraic_vjp.py.

docs.title: Backends and GPUs
docs.text:
Every backend runs the same compiled host program (C). They differ in how the parallel loops inside it are executed.

backend Parallel loops run on Notes "auto" the best multi-core strategy found default; same as "multicore" "c" the calling thread no threads at all; also compiles without parallel loop overhead "threads" Parakeet's persistent thread pool POSIX; fork-safe; no extra runtime library "gcd" Grand Central Dispatch macOS "openmp" the compiler's OpenMP runtime needs libgomp/libomp (macOS: brew install libomp) "metal" / "mps" the Apple GPU pip install "parakeet[metal]==1.0.0" "cuda" an NVIDIA GPU pip install "parakeet[cuda12]==1.0.0" (CuPy) "python" - runs the original function uncompiled 
parakeet.available_backends()
# {'python': 'ok', 'c': 'ok', 'threads': 'ok', 'gcd': 'ok', 'openmp': 'ok', 'metal': 'ok',
#  'cuda': 'unavailable: the CUDA backend needs CuPy, which is not installed. Install ...'}

A backend that cannot work fails when you select it, with a message saying what is missing and how to install it; not later with a linker error.

docs.title: Multi-core
docs.text:
Array expressions, map/allpairs/imap, comprehensions, parfor and reductions over recognised associative operations are split into chunks that run on parakeet.config.num_threads threads (default: all cores). Only the outermost data-parallel operation is parallelised; anything nested inside it runs sequentially within each thread.

Small loops are not worth a thread hand-off: loops with a cheap body run on the calling thread unless they have at least 2 * config.parallel_grain iterations (default 8192 per chunk). Loops whose body contains loops of its own are always split.

Compiled functions release the GIL and are safe to call from several Python threads at once. With multiprocessing, prefer the spawn start method when using "openmp" or "gcd" (those runtimes do not survive fork); the default thread pool does.

docs.title: Apple GPUs (Metal)
docs.text:
@jit(backend="metal")
def blur_energy(img):
  return (img[1:-1, 1:-1] * 4 - img[:-2, 1:-1] - img[2:, 1:-1] - img[1:-1, :-2] - img[1:-1, 2:]) ** 2

Each eligible parallel loop is also compiled to a Metal compute kernel; the host program hands loops of at least config.device_threshold iterations (default 32768) to the GPU and runs smaller ones on the CPU.

Apple GPUs have no float64

Metal does not support double precision. A loop that touches float64 data runs on the CPU thread pool instead, and Parakeet emits a FallbackWarning saying so. Pass float32 arrays and np.float32 scalars to stay on the GPU (a Python float argument is a double; x * 2.0 with a literal is fine).

Other reasons a loop stays on the CPU: it allocates temporary arrays per iteration, or it uses a function Metal lacks (lgamma, erfc). The warning always names the reason. Control this with config.device_fallback: "warn" (default), "silent", or "error" to refuse instead.

Runtime errors inside kernels (out-of-bounds indices, failed assertions) are reported as normal Python exceptions.

docs.title: NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA)
docs.text:
@jit(backend="cuda")
def distances(X, C):
  return parakeet.allpairs(lambda a, b: np.sum((a - b) ** 2), X, C)

Kernels are compiled at run time by CuPy's RawKernel (NVRTC), so only the NVIDIA driver and a CuPy wheel matching your CUDA version are needed. All dtypes including float64 are supported. The same per-loop fallback rules apply.

Validation status

CI has no NVIDIA hardware, so there the CUDA code generator runs against a simulator (PARAKEET_CUDA_SIMULATE=1) that compiles the generated kernels as C++ and executes their thread grid on the CPU.

The 1.0 release comparison ran on a physical NVIDIA A10 with strict device dispatch. Earlier checks on an A100 (Google Colab, CuPy with CUDA 13, Python 3.13) and Tesla T4 covered the whole test suite with every parallel loop forced onto the GPU (688 tests, including the tiled products, the gradient tests and arrays kept on the device between loops), the examples and the benchmarks all passed. That check is run on demand, not by CI:

pip install runplz google-colab-cli
runplz colab tools/colab_job.py          # T4; PK_COLAB_GPU=A100 for others

To push your own test suite through a GPU set PARAKEET_TEST_BACKENDS=cuda (the backends used by parakeet.testing.expect and check) and PARAKEET_DEVICE_THRESHOLD=1 (so small arrays go to the device too).

docs.title: What about TPUs?
docs.text: No. A TPU only runs programs compiled by XLA, which wants whole-array operations with static shapes; Parakeet generates scalar loops in C-like kernel languages. Parakeet's CPU backends do work on a Colab TPU host (24 x86 cores), which is all PK_COLAB_TPU=v5e1 runplz colab tools/colab_job.py checks.

docs.title: How data moves
docs.text:
Arrays belong to the host, but within one call they stay on the device.

  • The first GPU loop that uses an array puts it on the device. A buffer the host allocated and has not written to yet (the output of the loop, usually) is created there directly: nothing is copied. On Metal, arrays allocated by compiled code are shared with the GPU without copying at all.
  • Later loops find the array already there. What a loop wrote stays on the device; it is not copied back after every loop.
  • Host code that reads or writes array memory itself (an explicit Python loop, a loop that fell back to the CPU, a call into the BLAS) first asks for everything the device has changed. So does the end of the call.
  • A temporary that is freed before anyone on the host looked at it is never copied back.

A chain of array operations on a GPU therefore costs one upload of its inputs and one download of its result, however many loops it has. Mixing GPU loops with scalar host loops over the same arrays works, and gives the same answers, but pays for a download and an upload each time the two alternate.

Which loops go to the device. A loop is sent when its number of elements times the estimated inner iterations per element reaches config.device_threshold, and it has at least 1024 elements. A loop over 5,000 rows that each need a 10,000-step inner loop goes; a loop over 20,000 cheap elements stays on the CPU, where the launch would cost more than the work; so does a loop over 32 features however long each one's scan is, because a device runs one (slow) thread per element and 32 of them are no match for a few CPU cores.

Use parakeet.to_device(x, backend="cuda") or backend="metal" to reuse resident array inputs across calls. Pass the resulting device arrays to a compiled function and call parakeet.to_host(result) when Python needs the data. Operations which run on the host can still require transfers.

docs.title: Bioinformatics & structural biology
docs.text:
Scientific computing in genomics, cheminformatics, and structural biology is full of kernels that do not fit standard dense GEMM libraries: byte-level FASTQ parsing and 2-bit k-mer packing, multi-channel alignment pileups, 2048-bit chemical fingerprint screening, 3D protein coordinate message passing, and banded dynamic programming alignments.

Parakeet compiles these workloads directly from concise NumPy and data-parallel operators into fused, multi-core CPU and GPU code; without hand-writing C, CUDA, or Metal.

Every snippet below is included from examples/bio_gallery.py. Run the gallery checks or reproducible benchmarks from a source checkout:

python -m examples.bio_gallery
python benchmarks/bio_workloads.py

docs.title: How algebraic primitives map to bio workloads
docs.text: Domain task Operator / optimization in Parakeet What the compiler eliminates FASTQ k-mers & read QC par.parfor + uint8 / uint64 bitwise arithmetic Python per-character loops and string copies Multi-channel BAM pileup Keyed IndexScatter fusion Redundant passes over alignment positions (6 -> 1) Chemical fingerprint screening par.allpairs + ordered par.fold (pairwise_fold) O(N · M) similarity matrix allocation 3D protein RBF / equivariant attention Online rescaled-monoid tiling + par.grad O(N²) pairwise distance & weight matrices Banded Smith-Waterman & genome SSMs Two-row banded DP + chunkwise affine prefix scan (TileScan) Python DP interpreter overhead & sequential scan bottlenecks

docs.title: 1. FASTQ 2-bit canonical k-mers and read QC
docs.text:
Representing raw DNA and Phred quality bytes as uint8 arrays lets Parakeet compute forward and reverse-complement 2-bit uint64 canonical k-mers (min(fwd, revcomp)), GC fraction, and mean Phred quality in one parallel pass over reads:

@par.jit
def encode_canonical_kmers_and_gc(seq_bytes, qual_bytes, k):
  """Encode a batch of equal-length ASCII DNA reads (N, L) uint8 into:
  - canonical 2-bit k-mers (N, L - k + 1) uint64  [min(fwd, revcomp)]
  - per-read GC fraction (N,) float32
  - per-read mean Phred quality (N,) float32
  """
  n_reads, read_len = seq_bytes.shape
  n_kmers = read_len - k + 1
  kmers = np.empty((n_reads, n_kmers), dtype=np.uint64)
  gc_frac = np.empty((n_reads,), dtype=np.float32)
  mean_q = np.empty((n_reads,), dtype=np.float32)
  mask = (~np.uint64(0)) >> np.uint64(64 - 2 * k)
  rev_shift = np.uint64(2 * (k - 1))

  def process_read(r):
    gc = np.int64(0)
    qsum = np.int64(0)
    fwd = np.uint64(0)
    rev = np.uint64(0)
    for pos in range(read_len):
      ch = seq_bytes[r, pos]
      # ASCII: A=65 -> 0, C=67 -> 1, G=71 -> 2, T=84 -> 3
      is_c = ch == np.uint8(67)
      is_g = ch == np.uint8(71)
      is_t = ch == np.uint8(84)
      code = np.uint64(1) if is_c else (np.uint64(2) if is_g else (np.uint64(3) if is_t else np.uint64(0)))
      comp = np.uint64(3) ^ code
      if is_c or is_g:
        gc = gc + np.int64(1)
      qsum = qsum + np.int64(qual_bytes[r, pos]) - np.int64(33)
      fwd = ((fwd << np.uint64(2)) | code) & mask
      rev = (rev >> np.uint64(2)) | (comp << rev_shift)
      if pos >= k - 1:
        kmers[r, pos - k + 1] = fwd if fwd < rev else rev
    gc_frac[r] = np.float32(gc) / np.float32(read_len)
    mean_q[r] = np.float32(qsum) / np.float32(read_len)

  par.parfor(process_read, n_reads)
  return kmers, gc_frac, mean_q

docs.title: 2. Single-pass multi-channel alignment pileup
docs.text:
A pileup records A/C/G/T base counts, Phred quality sums, and reverse-strand counts at each reference coordinate. Because all six par.scatter_add updates share the same index array ref_pos, Parakeet's scatter-fusion pass combines them into a single privatized traversal (IndexScatter: 6 -> 1):

@par.jit
def single_pass_pileup(ref_pos, base_code, phred_q, is_rev, contig_len):
  """Accumulate A/C/G/T counts, quality sums, and reverse-strand counts across
  aligned base observations in one keyed IndexScatter traversal."""
  is_a = (base_code == np.uint8(0)).astype(np.int64)
  is_c = (base_code == np.uint8(1)).astype(np.int64)
  is_g = (base_code == np.uint8(2)).astype(np.int64)
  is_t = (base_code == np.uint8(3)).astype(np.int64)
  q_i64 = phred_q.astype(np.int64)
  rev_i64 = is_rev.astype(np.int64)

  # All six histograms share `ref_pos` -> Parakeet fuses them into ONE traversal!
  cnt_a = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_a)
  cnt_c = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_c)
  cnt_g = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_g)
  cnt_t = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, is_t)
  qual_sum = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, q_i64)
  rev_cnt = par.scatter_add(contig_len, ref_pos, rev_i64)
  return cnt_a, cnt_c, cnt_g, cnt_t, qual_sum, rev_cnt

docs.title: 3. 2048-bit Morgan fingerprint Tanimoto screening
docs.text:
Chemical similarity screening compares query fingerprints (N, 32) against a compound library (M, 32) of packed uint64 bitvectors (2,048 bits each). Combining a portable 64-bit SWAR popcount with par.allpairs and an ordered par.fold finds the closest library compound per query while preserving first-index ties:

def popcount64(x):
  """Branchless 64-bit SWAR popcount (portable across C, multicore, Metal, CUDA)."""
  u = x - ((x >> np.uint64(1)) & np.uint64(0x5555555555555555))
  u = (u & np.uint64(0x3333333333333333)) + ((u >> np.uint64(2)) & np.uint64(0x3333333333333333))
  u = (u + (u >> np.uint64(4))) & np.uint64(0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F)
  return (u * np.uint64(0x0101010101010101)) >> np.uint64(56)


class BestHit(NamedTuple):
  sim: np.float32
  index: np.int64


def better_hit(left, right):
  # Highest Tanimoto similarity wins; ties preserve the first library compound.
  return right if right.sim > left.sim else left


@par.jit
def tanimoto_nearest_hit(queries, library):
  """Find the closest library compound per query over packed uint64 fingerprints
  (N, W) x (M, W) using tiled pairwise folds with zero N x M allocation."""
  pop_q = np.sum(popcount64(queries), axis=1)
  pop_l = np.sum(popcount64(library), axis=1)

  def inter_bits(q_row, l_row):
    return np.sum(popcount64(q_row & l_row))

  # Stream intersection counts into an ordered fold over library compounds
  inter = par.allpairs(inter_bits, queries, library)
  denom = pop_q[:, None] + pop_l[None, :] - inter
  sim = np.where(
    denom > np.uint64(0), inter.astype(np.float32) / np.maximum(denom, np.uint64(1)).astype(np.float32), np.float32(0.0)
  )
  return par.fold(
    lambda score, ref_idx: BestHit(score, ref_idx),
    better_hit,
    sim,
    axis=1,
    indexed=True,
    emit=lambda hit: hit.index,
  )

docs.title: 4. 3D protein coordinate RBF message passing
docs.text:
Pairwise radial-basis-function smoothing over 3D residue coordinates (N, 3) uses the same rescaled-monoid structure as softmax attention. Online monoidal tiling fuses the squared-distance computation, softmax normalization, and feature aggregation into a single tiled pass with zero O(N²) score allocation; and par.grad differentiates through the 3D coordinates directly:

@par.jit
def protein_rbf_message_passing(coords, features, neg_inv_2sigma2):
  """3D radial-basis-function message passing over residue coordinates (N, 3).

  Fuses into online (m, l, O) monoidal tiles with zero N x N materialization.
  """
  d2 = np.sum((coords[:, None, :] - coords[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
  s = d2 * neg_inv_2sigma2
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ features


def protein_rbf_loss(coords, features, targets, neg_inv_2sigma2):
  pred = protein_rbf_message_passing(coords, features, neg_inv_2sigma2)
  diff = pred - targets
  return np.mean(diff * diff)


protein_coord_grad = par.grad(protein_rbf_loss, argnum=0)

docs.title: 5. Banded Smith-Waterman alignment and DNA state-space scan
docs.text:
Compiled two-row banded Smith-Waterman keeps only O(M) score scratch in L1 cache, while 1D DNA exponential state-space recurrences automatically rewrite into chunkwise parallel affine prefix scans (TileScan):

@par.jit
def banded_smith_waterman(seq_a, seq_b, match_score, mismatch_pen, gap_pen, band_width):
  """Banded Smith-Waterman local alignment score over integer-encoded sequences.

  Keeps only two O(M) score rows in cache and restricts columns to |j - i| <= band_width.
  """
  n = seq_a.shape[0]
  m = seq_b.shape[0]
  prev = np.zeros((m + 1,), dtype=np.float32)
  curr = np.zeros((m + 1,), dtype=np.float32)
  best = np.float32(0.0)
  for i in range(1, n + 1):
    ai = seq_a[i - 1]
    j_lo = i - band_width
    if j_lo < 1:
      j_lo = 1
    j_hi = i + band_width
    if j_hi > m:
      j_hi = m
    for j in range(j_lo, j_hi + 1):
      sub = match_score if ai == seq_b[j - 1] else mismatch_pen
      v = prev[j - 1] + sub
      up = prev[j] + gap_pen
      left = curr[j - 1] + gap_pen
      if up > v:
        v = up
      if left > v:
        v = left
      if v < np.float32(0.0):
        v = np.float32(0.0)
      curr[j] = v
      if v > best:
        best = v
    for j in range(j_lo, j_hi + 1):
      prev[j] = curr[j]
      curr[j] = np.float32(0.0)
  return best


@par.jit
def dna_ssm_scan(decay, signal):
  """Exponential state-space scan along a DNA track (L,).

  Compiled via chunkwise parallel affine prefix scan (TileScan).
  """
  length = decay.shape[0]
  out = np.empty_like(signal)
  s = np.float32(0.0)
  for t in range(length):
    s = decay[t] * s + signal[t]
    out[t] = s
  return out

docs.title: Lists, growable CPU vectors, & GPU scratch stacks
docs.text:
• Compile-time static list: Straight-line and unrolled outs = [] with .append(), .extend(), .pop(), .clear(), indexing/slicing, and consumption by np.stack, np.concatenate, np.array, and RaggedArray.from_sequences lowers away before IR emission and composes seamlessly with par.grad.
  • Runtime growable CPU list[T]: Lists mutated inside runtime for/while loops or dynamic if branches automatically promote to a refcounted homogeneous growable buffer (buf, len, cap) with geometric doubling and zero-copy conversion to ArrayVal (par.config.verify=True clean).
  • par.fixed_list(capacity, dtype): Fixed-capacity stack-allocated scratch buffer (ir.Alloc(..., stack=True)) emitted natively as thread-local stack arrays on CPU, multicore, CUDA, and Apple Metal with zero malloc and runtime bounds/capacity checks.
  • Dynamic-shape loop rebinding: Verified runtime shape rebinding for both ArrayVal (e.g., arr = arr[arr > thresh]) and RaggedArray across while and for loops under par.config.verify=True.
  • Static itertools & generators: Zero-allocation compilation for itertools.pairwise, itertools.islice, itertools.chain, itertools.product, and itertools.batched in for loops and generator expressions (sum(...), np.array(...)).

docs.title: 1.4.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Broader idiomatic Python semantics lowered cleanly at elaboration time with zero PyObject overhead: non-frozen @dataclass records with pure methods, @property, __call__, and functional field rebinding; full structural match/case destructuring; compile-time isinstance/hasattr/getattr dead-branch pruning; and *args/**kwargs, functools.partial, and operator.* call ergonomics (Python Semantics Wave 1, closing #79).

docs.title: Non-frozen @dataclass, methods & @property
docs.text:
• Non-frozen @dataclass records: Both frozen and regular @dataclass objects compile to unboxed compile-time records across @par.jit, par.grad, and par.jvp (with discrete metadata fields treated as zero-tangent static leaves).
  • Functional local field rebinding: obj.x = new_x, nested obj.a.b = v, and augmented updates obj.x += v rebuild the compile-time record chain functionally (value semantics, zero heap mutation); including across loops and branches.
  • Pure methods, @property, @staticmethod, @classmethod, & __call__: Methods and properties on @dataclass and NamedTuple records inline like ordinary helper functions; bound methods on records can also be passed directly from Python into @par.jit and par.map.

docs.title: Structural match/case, isinstance/hasattr, & call ergonomics
docs.text:
• Extended structural match/case: Added MatchMapping (case {"k": v, **rest}:), starred array patterns (case [first, *mid, last]:), and class patterns for non-frozen dataclasses, RaggedArray, np.ndarray, dict, and tuple.
  • Compile-time isinstance, hasattr, & getattr: Resolved statically against the specialization key (including Python 3.10+ union types A | B, user dataclasses, NamedTuple, and RaggedArray) with guaranteed dead-branch pruning.
  • Call ergonomics: Full **kwargs collection and **d unpacking, functools.partial (both inside @par.jit and passed from Python), and operator.* callables (operator.add, operator.mul, operator.itemgetter, operator.attrgetter, etc.) including associative par.reduce/par.scan combiners.

docs.title: 1.3.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Composable forward-mode, general reverse-mode, and higher-order automatic differentiation (jvp, vjp, linearize, linear_transpose, hvp, jacfwd, jacrev, hessian, @custom_jvp), zero-$O(T^2)$ rematerialized attention JVP/HVP, idiomatic np.add.at and for-loop scatter lifting, and a documentation and examples overhaul (AD Upgrade Wave 2, closing #76, #77, and #78).

docs.title: Forward-mode AD, general VJPs & linear transposes
docs.text:
• par.jvp & @par.custom_jvp: Symbolic forward-mode differentiation over scalars, arrays, matmul/einsum, reductions (tie-averaged min/max, zero-safe prod), scans, folds, map, gather/scatter, if/else, runtime for/while loops (in $O(1)$ extra memory), NamedTuple / frozen @dataclass records, and RaggedArrays.
  • General non-scalar par.vjp, par.linearize, & par.linear_transpose: Full reverse-mode pullbacks for array, tuple, record, and RaggedArray outputs, plus exact linear operator transposes satisfying ⟨JVP(x; v), u⟩ == ⟨v, VJP(x; u)⟩.
  • Higher-order AD (par.hvp, par.jacfwd, par.jacrev, par.hessian): Forward-over-reverse Hessian-vector products across MLPs, LayerNorm, checkpointed for loops, and FlashAttention. Also lifted reverse-over-reverse grad(grad(...)) cliffs for np.stack, np.cumsum, gather indexing, scatter-add, and scalar 1-to-1 par.map.

docs.title: Composable algebraic AD & indexing adjoints
docs.text:
• Zero-$O(T^2)$ attention JVP & HVP: Fused dual (S, dS) -> (O, dO) monoidal tiling and parallel rematerialized HVP tangent emission drop all quadratic $O(T^2)$ allocations during both par.jvp and par.hvp (reported by par.show_rewrite).
  • Composable ALGEBRAIC_AD_RULES registry: Unified FlashAttention, Cut Cross-Entropy, softmax, and LayerNorm / RMSNorm rematerialization rules and enabled algebraic tape optimization inside checkpointed runtime for loops.
  • topk, sort, FrozenHashTable, & SortedIndex AD: Added reverse-mode and forward-mode differentiation for par.topk / par.topk_fold, np.sort, FrozenHashTable.get, and SortedIndex.get.
  • Multi-store vertical fusion fix: Hardened match_single_output_map and match_single_output_scan to reject multi-store prefixes, fixing a compiler bug exposed by fused primal+tangent IndexMaps.

docs.title: Idiomatic scatter lowering & documentation overhaul
docs.text:
• np.add.at and for-loop scatter lifting: np.add.at(out, idx, vals) and canonical for i in range(n): out[idx[i]] += vals[i] loops (including multi-histogram bodies sharing an index binding b = bin_ids[i]) now lift directly to IndexScatter, fuse sibling histograms into one privatized traversal, and differentiate cleanly under both grad and jvp.
  • Consistent NumPy idioms & pedagogical gallery: Standardized docs and examples on np.* helpers (np.minimum, np.add, np.add.at, etc.) alongside @par.jit / par.* operators, replaced bare Law 1..6 shorthand outside docs/algebra.md with plain-English optimization descriptions, and reordered the Kernel gallery progressively from pairwise NumPy fusion to attention and end-to-end training.

docs.title: 1.2.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Major automatic differentiation upgrade: IR-level checkpointed reverse loops for runtime-bound for/while loops, par.fold, and general par.scan, plus par.stop_gradient, @par.custom_vjp, and @par.checkpoint (AD Upgrade Wave 1, closing #75 and advancing #77).

docs.title: Reverse-mode AD through runtime & long loops
docs.text:
• IR-level $O(\sqrt{T})$ checkpointed reverse for loops: Loops over runtime-length ranges or arrays (for t in range(T):, for t in range(weights.shape[0]):) and long static loops (> 32 iterations) compile once to a two-level checkpointed reverse loop in IR without unrolling or recompiling per length, removing the MAX_UNROLL = 4096 cliff.
  • IR-level $O(\log T)$ checkpointed reverse while loops: Runtime-converging while loops (fixed-point solvers, adaptive ODE/relaxation steps) now differentiate through a fixed-slot (64 slots) stride-doubling online checkpoint schedule with bounded memory.
  • Checkpointed $O(\sqrt{N})$ par.fold & differentiable general par.scan: Arbitrary non-monoidal par.reduce/par.fold and 1-D par.scan now differentiate via checkpointed reverse segments without storing full $O(N)$ histories.
  • Rewrite inspection: par.show_rewrite(par.grad(...), ...) now reports AD: Checkpointed Reverse Loop when checkpointed reverse loops are emitted.

docs.title: Explicit AD control primitives
docs.text:
• par.stop_gradient(x): Zero-copy gradient barrier across scalars, arrays, tuples, RaggedArray, and records (for straight-through estimators, target networks, and stop-gradient RL losses).
  • @par.custom_vjp (.defvjp(fwd, bwd)): User-defined reverse-mode rules supporting multi-output pytree values, auxiliary residuals, and higher-order differentiation.
  • @par.checkpoint (rematerialization): Explicit activation checkpointing that re-runs the forward block during backpropagation while composing cleanly with Law 2 FlashAttention / LayerNorm rematerialization.
  • Record static metadata leaves: Non-float fields inside NamedTuple and frozen @dataclass records now pass through AD as zero-tangent static leaves.

docs.title: 1.1.0 (November 25, 2026)
docs.text: Major expansion of Parakeet's GPU schedules, algebraic data structures, scientific/bioinformatics primitives, and documentation; unified under one top-level import parakeet as par (@par.jit, par.*) interface.

docs.title: Unified namespace, docs & benchmarks
docs.text:
• Single unified parakeet namespace: Exported fold, topk, topk_fold, tanimoto_topk, ipa_attention, show_rewrite, RewriteReport, scatter, iscan, iscatter, and ifilter_reduce directly on top-level parakeet (with parakeet.dsl retained as a backward-compatible alias). Standardized examples and docs on import parakeet as par (@par.jit, par.*).
  • Reproducible benchmark figures & overhaul: Added tools/gen_benchmark_figures.py generating per-replicate scatter + IQR + median SVGs (bench-pairwise-l4.svg, bench-scaling-1nn.svg, bench-workloads-l4.svg) directly from docs/assets/colab-l4-0dcb7d5.json, reorganized the Benchmarks page by workload category, connected README.md directly to runnable implementations, and updated the NYU history links (Rubinsteyn 2014 thesis, Hielscher et al. 2013 arXiv:1304.1835, HotPar '12).
  • Bioinformatics & structural biology guide: Added the Bioinformatics & structural biology gallery (examples/bio_gallery.py) and reproducible benchmark suite (benchmarks/bio_workloads.py).

docs.title: GPU schedules & matrix units
docs.text:
• Tiled GPU pairwise folds: Broadcasting NumPy and nested-map/structured par.fold exact 1-NN and inverse-distance smoothing now stream shared-memory score tiles (16 KiB/block) on CUDA and Metal with exact first-index tie and NaN semantics; 4.8× faster (2.60 ms → 0.54 ms) and 21× less global scratch (64 MiB → 3 MiB) at 1,024 × 16,384 × 32 on NVIDIA L4.
  • Hardware matrix units in monoidal kernels: Enabled Metal simdgroup_matrix and CUDA TF32 WMMA inside Law 1 rescaled-monoid kernels (FlashAttention, RBF, linear cross-entropy, nanoGPT training).
  • Device-resident GPU scans & reductions: Kept GPU prefix scans, small GPU reductions, and extrema values device-resident without host round-trips.

docs.title: New algebraic primitives & data structures
docs.text:
• First-class RaggedArray (CSR) & segmented operators: RaggedArray, segment_ids, segmented_map, segmented_reduce, segmented_scan, segmented_softmax, and differentiable varlen_flash_attention with ragged reverse-mode AD (par.grad preserves offsets structurally).
  • 1-to-K ragged compaction (IndexExpand): Added par.flatmap and par.filter_pairs (two-pass count → prefix-sum → emit) with dead-output elimination and AD gather support.
  • Parallel sorting, search & lookup tables: Parallel radix sort / argsort / unique, fusible searchsorted, SortedIndex, and static open-addressed FrozenHashTable.
  • 3D spatial pruning & block-sparse attention (Law 5 generalized): morton_order, 3D AABB spatial_cutoff_sum, and CSR BlockMask block_sparse_attention with forward + backward AD.
  • 2D / banded semiring DP (IndexWavefront): Added par.wavefront, par.batched_wavefront, and Law 2 checkpointed differentiable par.soft_align (Smith-Waterman / Needleman-Wunsch / soft-DTW).
  • Vector-valued Carry folds & pair-biased / IPA attention: Multi-slot Carry folds powering exact par.topk, par.topk_fold, par.tanimoto_topk, and Law 1+2 par.ipa_attention.
  • Zero-copy bytes, bitops & Python ergonomics: Zero-copy uint8 bytes / mmap inputs, popcount/clz/ctz/rotl/rotr/bswap, bf16_to_f32 / f32_to_bf16, IntEnum, scalar match/case, frozen @dataclass dataclasses.replace, and structured NumPy views.

docs.title: 1.0.0 (November 24, 2026)
docs.text: A ground-up rewrite for modern Python. The @jit decorator, the adverbs (map, reduce, scan, allpairs, imap, ...) and the overall idea are unchanged; everything underneath is new.

docs.title: Algebraic operators
docs.text:
• The same CPU tile schedule serves exact nearest-neighbor queries written as broadcasting NumPy or nested parallel maps. It merges a distance and index per query and preserves the first index on ties.
  • Two weighted histograms over shared bin IDs can fuse into a single traversal. Structured folds accept tuples and named records with a user-defined merge.
  • Algebraic rewrites cover online normalized sums, their gradients, reassociation of contractions, and chunked affine scans. The rewrite inspector shows which passes fired for a given function and input.
  • The gallery includes runnable examples. The release benchmarks compare five workloads with general-purpose and specialist implementations on a four-vCPU worker and an NVIDIA A10.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• grad and value_and_grad: reverse-mode differentiation as an adverb. Element-wise operators, reductions, matrix products, views, map and allpairs with your own functions all have derivative rules; loops of known length are unrolled; anything without a rule raises instead of returning a wrong gradient. examples/nanogpt.py and examples/convnet.py train with it.
  • More of grad: cumsum, sort, einsum, stacks of matrices, folds with any function, and if statements on run-time conditions (both branches run, results are selected). The derivative of a map runs in parallel.
  • A middle end: elaboration now produces operator statements (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, printed by spec.operators) and a pipeline of passes rewrites them before they become loops. Tiling is one such pass, a pattern match on the IR instead of a trial elaboration; vertical fusion (Map→Map including matmul epilogues, Scan→Map into emit, Map→Filter, Map→Reduce), filter fusion (Filter→Filter and Filter→Reduce: np.sum(x[x > 0]) is one loop and allocates nothing), sibling fusion (x.min(), x.max() and np.sin(x), np.cos(x) each share one loop), reduction interchange (np.sum(X, axis=0) becomes L1-tiled contiguous SIMD loops), and dead-operator elimination all run at this level; find_broken_transform bisects the pass list; config.skip_transforms switches passes off.
  • General operators: reduce, scan and filter take several arrays with map= (and emit=); np.einsum; @ on stacks; reductions over several axes in one pass; tiling for maps of any rank.
  • Parallel primitives: prefix scans (cumsum), filters (x[mask], nonzero) and argmin/argmax run in parallel, on CPUs and GPUs.
  • GPU: arrays stay on the device between the loops of one call; a loop is sent to the device by the work in it, not its element count.
  • BLAS: float matrix products call the BLAS NumPy uses.
  • Tiling: two-dimensional maps of reductions (@, allpairs distances, ...) run a cache-sized tile at a time with their reductions jammed 2×4. A 1024×1024 matrix product is 2× faster on one core and 3× on all of them.
  • np.sort and np.argsort take axis and sort every lane in parallel (N-d input used to be flattened without saying so).
  • The dimensions of an array argument can be compile-time constants when the code needs them to be (range(w.shape[0]) in a loop that must be unrolled).
  • parakeet.macro and parakeet.find_broken_transform are back, and the code is laid out in frontend/, syntax/, transforms/ and lib/ again.
  • Faster compiles for large functions: identical loop bodies are compiled once.
  • Checked on real NVIDIA hardware. The whole suite passes with every parallel loop forced onto a Tesla T4 (tools/colab_job.py, run on demand with runplz colab; not part of CI).
  • Reads like Parakeet again: two-space indentation, parakeet.prims and parakeet.ndtypes, and the 0.x helpers typed_repr, specialize, run_python_fn, openmp_available, rank/size/shape, plus the old config.opt_fusion / config.print_* option names.

  • Fixed: two arguments of one GPU kernel that view the same memory now share a device buffer (previously one of them could read a truncated copy).

  • Python 3.11+ and NumPy 2, no dependencies besides NumPy and a C compiler (the dsltools, appdirs, llvmpy and PyCUDA dependencies are gone).

  • New frontend. Functions are elaborated directly into a typed loop IR: calls are inlined, closures/tuples/slices are resolved at compile time, and array expressions are fused into their consumers.
  • Backends: sequential C; multi-core through a built-in thread pool, OpenMP or Grand Central Dispatch; Apple GPUs through Metal; NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA (CuPy/NVRTC, no nvcc needed). GPU backends fall back to the CPU per loop, with a warning that says why.
  • NumPy-exact typing (NEP 50): result dtypes match NumPy, including the treatment of Python scalars.
  • Safety: bounds checks, shape checks, division and domain checks raise the same exceptions NumPy/Python would; compile errors carry the source location and the chain of inlined calls; reference-counted temporaries are freed eagerly (no more leaks in loops).
  • Much larger language subset: early return, break/continue, while, keyword/default/*args arguments, walrus, assert/raise, boolean-mask and integer-array indexing (reads and writes), in-place operators with NumPy aliasing semantics, 0-d and empty arrays, all integer/float dtypes.
  • Much larger library: ~200 NumPy functions and methods, np.random (a counter-based generator that is reproducible in parallel and on GPUs), sorting, math, and most numeric builtins.
  • Globals and closure variables are read at call time (no stale constants); arguments that must be compile-time constants (such as axis) are specialised on demand.
  • Compiled modules are cached on disk and shared between processes.
  • parakeet.config, parakeet.options(...), PARAKEET_* environment variables, f.specialize(...).ir/.source/.kernels, available_backends().
