docs.title: Compile-time errors
docs.text:
Everything Parakeet cannot compile is reported when the function is first called with a given set of argument types, as a subclass of parakeet.CompileError:

Exception Meaning UnsupportedError a Python or NumPy feature outside the supported subset TypeInferenceError (also a TypeError) types that cannot be reconciled, wrong arguments StaticValueError (also a ValueError) something that must be a compile-time constant is not, or is invalid

The message carries the source line, a caret under the offending expression, and (because calls are inlined) the chain of calls that led there:

parakeet.errors.TypeInferenceError: indices must be a scalar, got str 'a'
  File "model.py", line 15, in helper
    return v[k] * 2
           ^^^^
called from
  File "model.py", line 21, in outer
    total += helper(x, "a")
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

err.location and err.call_chain give the same information programmatically, and a note records the argument types being compiled.

docs.title: Run-time errors
docs.text:
Generated code raises ordinary exceptions, with a note pointing at the source line that failed:

@jit
def third(x):
  return x[2]


third(np.zeros(2))
# IndexError: index 2 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 2
#   raised by compiled code at demo.py:5 (in third)
Situation Exception index out of range IndexError shapes that do not broadcast, bad reshape, ragged map results, empty reduction without identity ValueError //, % or / by zero on Python numbers ZeroDivisionError assert AssertionError allocation failure MemoryError writing to a read-only array ValueError

Checks are also performed inside parallel loops and GPU kernels. When an error occurs, temporaries allocated so far are released.

NumPy array arithmetic follows NumPy: integer division by zero yields 0 and floating-point operations yield inf/nan rather than raising.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
backend="python" : Run the original function. If the answer is still wrong the bug is in your code, not in the compiler: f(x, _backend="python").

f.specialize(*args) : Compile for example arguments without running and return a Specialization: .operators (maps and reductions over index spaces, as elaborated), .ir (typed loop IR after the passes), .source (C), .kernels (GPU kernel sources), .signature.

f.inspect(*args) : Print the IR.

parakeet.config.print_ir, parakeet.config.print_code : Print the IR / C of everything as it is compiled (also PARAKEET_PRINT_IR=1).

@jit(fusion=False) : Evaluate every array expression into its own temporary. Useful to check whether a problem is related to loop fusion.

parakeet.find_broken_transform(fn, inputs) : Switch the optimizations on one at a time; fusion, each pass of the middle end (dead code, vertical fusion, filter fusion, sibling fusion, reduction interchange, tiling), the C optimizer, parallel loops, the GPU; and name the first one that makes the result differ from plain Python (or from expected, if given).

parakeet.clear_cache() : Delete cached compiled modules (they are keyed by the generated source and compiler, so this is never needed for correctness).

If you hit a parakeet.errors.InternalError or a CCompilerError, that is a bug in Parakeet: the message includes where the generated source was kept. Please open an issue with it.

docs.title: Kernel gallery
docs.text:
Parakeet compiles ordinary NumPy code, plain Python loops, and explicit data-parallel operators (par.map, par.allpairs, par.fold, par.imap, par.ireduce, par.scatter_add) through the same @par.jit decorator and the same algebraic IR.

How this page is organized: the examples progress from straightforward pairwise NumPy fusion and histograms to custom semiring reductions, parallel recurrences, and modern attention and loss kernels; introducing Parakeet's capabilities one layer at a time. Where a section has tabs, those tabs show alternative ways to write the exact same computation (idiomatic NumPy vs. plain loops vs. explicit Parakeet operators) that all compile to the same fused, tiled schedule.

For a complete end-to-end training walkthrough, see nanoGPT. For genomics, cheminformatics, and 3D protein kernels, see Bioinformatics & structural biology. For the underlying identities behind these rewrites, see Algebraic laws.

Every snippet below is included directly from examples/algebraic_gallery.py and verified by python -m examples.algebraic_gallery.

from typing import NamedTuple
import numpy as np
import parakeet as par

docs.title: Exact nearest neighbor
docs.text:
Exact nearest-neighbor search finds, for each of Q query vectors in $\mathbb{R}^D$, the index of the closest vector among R reference vectors under Euclidean distance. Writing this with broadcasting NumPy is two lines, but executing it eagerly allocates a full Q × R distance matrix; 64 MiB at Q = 1,024, R = 16,384; that thrashes cache and GPU memory.

Parakeet fuses the distance calculation directly into an ordered tiled reduction across R, keeping only a small score tile in L1 cache or GPU shared memory (16 KiB per block) and preserving NumPy's exact first-index rule on equal-distance ties and NaNs.

Broadcasting NumPyNested par.map and np.argminpar.allpairs and structured par.fold 
@par.jit
def nearest_numpy(queries, references):
  delta = queries[:, None, :] - references[None, :, :]
  return np.argmin(np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2), axis=1)

For each query row, map the squared distance over all reference rows and take np.argmin. The outer par.map runs that search in parallel across queries.

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return np.sum((query - reference) ** np.float32(2))



@par.jit
def exact_1nn(x_query, x_ref):
  """Exact nearest-neighbor index per query row."""
  return par.map(
    lambda query: np.argmin(par.map(lambda reference: squared_distance(query, reference), x_ref)),
    x_query,
  )

Define the logical Q × R domain with par.allpairs, pack each (distance, index) pair into a NamedTuple, and reduce with an explicit associative merge rule (first_minimum).

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return np.sum((query - reference) ** np.float32(2))



class Winner(NamedTuple):
  distance: np.float32
  index: np.int64


def first_minimum(left, right):
  # Keep the first NaN. Among finite values, replace only on strict improvement.
  right_wins = np.isnan(right.distance) or right.distance < left.distance
  return right if right_wins and not np.isnan(left.distance) else left


@par.jit
def nearest_fold(queries, references):
  scores = par.allpairs(squared_distance, queries, references)
  return par.fold(Winner, first_minimum, scores, axis=1, indexed=True, emit=lambda winner: winner.index)

All three spellings compile to the same tiled pairwise schedule on CPU, Metal, and CUDA without allocating the Q × R distance matrix. Compare timings, scaling, and scratch memory.

docs.title: Inverse-distance smoothing
docs.text:
Swap the fold state from (min_distance, index) to (weight_sum, weighted_sum) and the same squared distances predict a smoothed scalar observation at each query with weight $w_{ij} = 1 / (1 + |q_i - r_j|^2)$. Parakeet computes each distance once, sums both fields inside each tile, and divides the totals after the final merge.

Broadcasting NumPypar.allpairs and par.fold 
@par.jit
def smooth_numpy(queries, references, observations):
  observations = observations.reshape(references.shape[0])
  delta = queries[:, None, :] - references[None, :, :]
  weights = 1 / (1 + np.sum(delta ** np.float32(2), axis=2))
  return np.sum(weights * observations, axis=1) / np.sum(weights, axis=1)

def squared_distance(query, reference):
  return np.sum((query - reference) ** np.float32(2))



class WeightedSum(NamedTuple):
  weight: np.float32
  weighted_value: np.float32


def add_sums(left, right):
  return WeightedSum(left.weight + right.weight, left.weighted_value + right.weighted_value)


@par.jit
def smooth_fold(queries, references, observations):
  values = observations.reshape(references.shape[0])
  scores = par.allpairs(squared_distance, queries, references)

  def contribution(distance_squared, ref_index):
    weight = 1 / (1 + distance_squared)
    return WeightedSum(weight, weight * values[ref_index])

  def weighted_mean(total):
    return total.weighted_value / total.weight

  return par.fold(contribution, add_sums, scores, axis=1, indexed=True, emit=weighted_mean)

docs.title: Gaussian kernel regression
docs.text:
Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression predicts each query's target vector by weighting reference observations with a Gaussian kernel $\exp(-\gamma |q_i - x_j|^2)$. Because the running maximum, weight sum, and weighted output form an associative rescaled monoid, Parakeet streams references in tiles instead of allocating an N × M weight matrix; the exact same online monoidal pass that powers tiled attention below.

@par.jit
def rbf_kernel_regression(x_query, x_train, y_train, neg_gamma):
  d2 = np.sum((x_query[:, None, :] - x_train[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
  s = d2 * neg_gamma
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ y_train

docs.title: Histograms and tree splits
docs.text:
Histogram-based gradient boosted trees accumulate gradients and Hessians into feature bins, scan cumulative left/right sums, and pick the split bin with the highest gain. You can write the bin accumulations as a declarative NumPy comprehension, with np.add.at, as a plain Python for loop, or with explicit par.scatter_add (including keyed generator expressions); all four lower to Parakeet's $O(N)$ IndexScatter operator. Because both accumulations share the same bin_ids array, Parakeet fuses them into a single thread-privatized traversal over the observations.

Declarative comprehensionNumPy np.add.atPython for loopExplicit par.scatter_add

A pull-style comprehension [np.sum(grads[bin_ids == b]) for b in range(nbins)] (or [sum(grads[i] for i in range(len(bin_ids)) if bin_ids[i] == b) for b in range(nbins)]) would cost $O(\text{nbins} \cdot N)$ naively. Parakeet inverts it automatically to an $O(N)$ IndexScatter and fuses both histograms into one pass.

@par.jit
def gbdt_best_split_comprehension(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Declarative pull-style comprehension inverted to one fused O(N) scatter."""
  g_hist = np.array([np.sum(grads[bin_ids == b]) for b in range(nbins)])
  h_hist = np.array([np.sum(hess[bin_ids == b]) for b in range(nbins)])
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_right = g_left[nbins - 1] - g_left
  h_right = h_left[nbins - 1] - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

@par.jit
def gbdt_best_split_numpy(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Return the split bin with the highest gain and the gain at that bin."""
  g_hist = np.zeros(nbins, dtype=np.float32)
  h_hist = np.zeros(nbins, dtype=np.float32)
  np.add.at(g_hist, bin_ids, grads)
  np.add.at(h_hist, bin_ids, hess)
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_right = g_left[nbins - 1] - g_left
  h_right = h_left[nbins - 1] - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

When an indexed += loop writes only into fresh buffers that are never read inside the loop, Parakeet proves independence, lifts each update to IndexScatter, and fuses sibling histograms sharing b = bin_ids[i] into one parallel traversal automatically.

@par.jit
def gbdt_best_split_loop(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Same histogram split written with a plain Python accumulation loop."""
  g_hist = np.zeros(nbins, dtype=np.float32)
  h_hist = np.zeros(nbins, dtype=np.float32)
  for i in range(len(bin_ids)):
    b = bin_ids[i]
    g_hist[b] += grads[i]
    h_hist[b] += hess[i]
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_right = g_left[nbins - 1] - g_left
  h_right = h_left[nbins - 1] - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

@par.jit
def gbdt_best_split(bin_ids, grads, hess, nbins, reg_lambda):
  """Return the split bin with the highest gain and the gain at that bin."""
  g_hist = par.scatter_add(nbins, bin_ids, grads)
  h_hist = par.scatter_add(nbins, bin_ids, hess)
  g_left = np.cumsum(g_hist)
  h_left = np.cumsum(h_hist)
  g_tot = g_left[nbins - 1]
  h_tot = h_left[nbins - 1]
  g_right = g_tot - g_left
  h_right = h_tot - h_left
  gain = (g_left * g_left) / (h_left + reg_lambda) + (g_right * g_right) / (h_right + reg_lambda)
  best_bin = np.argmax(gain)
  return best_bin, gain[best_bin]

docs.title: Min-plus matrix product
docs.text:
In shortest-path and tropical algebra, matrix multiplication replaces (*, +) with (+, min): $C_{ij} = \min_r (A_{ir} + B_{rj})$. Writing the index space explicitly with par.imap and par.ireduce(..., combine=np.minimum) avoids an m × n × k broadcast tensor and triggers the same cache and register tiling as standard matrix multiplication.

@par.jit
def tropical_min_plus(a, b):
  """One min-plus matrix product: C[i, j] = min_r (A[i, r] + B[r, j])."""
  m, k = a.shape
  _, n = b.shape
  return par.imap(
    lambda i, j: par.ireduce(lambda r: a[i, r] + b[r, j], k, combine=np.minimum),
    (m, n),
  )

docs.title: Exponential IIR filter
docs.text:
A plain Python for t in range(T): affine recurrence s = a[t] * s + b[t] has O(T) serial depth. Because affine maps compose associatively, Parakeet's chunkwise scan pass rewrites the loop into a parallel prefix scan (TileScan) across CPU cores or GPU threadblocks with no O(T) scratch arrays.

@par.jit
def iir_exponential_filter(a, b):
  T = a.shape[0]
  out = np.empty_like(b)
  s = np.float32(0.0)
  for t in range(T):
    s = a[t] * s + b[t]
    out[t] = s
  return out

docs.title: Mamba-2 state-space recurrence
docs.text:
The same chunkwise state-space duality generalizes to bilinear matrix-state recurrences: a 6-line Python loop over time rewrites into division-free chunkwise batched GEMMs that automatically lower to CPU register tiling, Metal simdgroup_matrix, and CUDA TF32 WMMA.

@par.jit
def mamba2_ssd(q, k, v, a):
  T = q.shape[0]
  out = np.empty((T, v.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
  S = np.zeros((k.shape[1], v.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
  for t in range(T):
    S = a[t] * S + k[t][:, None] * v[t][None, :]
    out[t] = q[t] @ S
  return out

docs.title: Causal attention
docs.text:
Write scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask in six lines of NumPy. Three general passes compose automatically:

  • Online monoidal tiling fuses the softmax-weighted contraction into a single streaming pass with no T × T score matrix (details).
  • Tile-interval mask pruning proves upper-triangular tiles are completely masked and skips loading their keys and values (details).
  • Rematerialized differentiation recomputes score tiles on the fly during par.grad, par.jvp, and par.hvp instead of storing T × T tensors (details).
@par.jit
def causal_flash_attention(q, k, v):
  T = q.shape[-2]
  idx = np.arange(T)
  mask = idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :]
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = np.where(mask, np.matmul(q, np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2)) * scale, np.float32(-1e9))
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return np.matmul(e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True), v)

For a sliding window, intersect the mask with (idx[:, None] - idx[None, :]) <= window; interval analysis skips tiles outside the window automatically.

docs.title: Linear cross-entropy
docs.text:
Computing cross-entropy over a large vocabulary V from hidden states h @ w normally materializes an M × V logit matrix. Online monoidal tiling chunks the contraction and logsumexp over the vocabulary while gathering the target logit on the fly, and algebraic rematerialization differentiates the loss with zero M × V memory.

def cut_cross_entropy(h, w, targets):
  logits = h @ w
  m = np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
  z = logits - m
  lse = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z), axis=-1))
  picked = z[np.arange(h.shape[0]), targets]
  return -np.mean(picked - lse)

docs.title: Multi-head latent attention
docs.text:
Multi-head latent attention (MLA) projects keys and values from a shared low-rank latent c_kv. When the query length is small (such as autoregressive decoding), bilinear contraction reassociation absorbs w_uk into q and defers w_uv until after attention; running tiled attention directly over the compressed latent c_kv.

@par.jit
def deepseek_mla(q, c_kv, w_uk, w_uv):
  k = c_kv @ w_uk
  v = c_kv @ w_uv
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = (q @ k.T) * scale
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ v

docs.title: Grouped-query attention
docs.text:
When a head-group axis G in q broadcasts against a single shared KV head (1 in k and v), shared-KV head-group tiling folds G into the query tile so all G query heads reuse one shared-memory load of k and v.

@par.jit
def gqa_attention(q, k, v):
  # q: (B, H_kv, G, T_q, D), k, v: (B, H_kv, 1, T_kv, D)
  scale = np.float32(1.0 / np.sqrt(np.float32(q.shape[-1])))
  s = np.matmul(q, np.swapaxes(k, -1, -2)) * scale
  e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
  return np.matmul(e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True), v)

docs.title: Dataclasses, methods, and polymorphic dispatch
docs.text:
Parakeet lowers @dataclass records (frozen or non-frozen), pure methods, @property, __call__, structural match/case, compile-time isinstance, functools.partial, and *args/**kwargs away completely during elaboration - letting you write idiomatic scientific Python types that still compile to fused, tiled, differentiable native code (examples/protein_and_layers.py):

@dataclass
class ProteinBackbone:
  """Mutable-style @dataclass with pure methods, @property, and functional field updates."""

  coords: np.ndarray  # (N, 3, 3) for N, CA, C atoms per residue
  residue_ids: np.ndarray  # (N,) int64 metadata (zero-tangent static leaf under AD)
  chain_name: str = "A"

  @property
  def ca_coords(self):
    return self.coords[:, 1, :]

  @property
  def n_residues(self):
    return self.coords.shape[0]

  def centered(self):
    mu = np.mean(self.ca_coords, axis=0, keepdims=True)
    self.coords = self.coords - mu[:, None, :]
    return self

  def rbf_message_passing(self, features, neg_gamma):
    ca = self.ca_coords
    d2 = np.sum((ca[:, None, :] - ca[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2.0), axis=-1)
    s = d2 * neg_gamma
    e = np.exp(s - np.max(s, axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return (e / np.sum(e, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) @ features


@dataclass
class MLPBlock:
  """Callable @dataclass layer with polymorphic dense/ragged dispatch."""

  w1: np.ndarray
  b1: np.ndarray
  w2: np.ndarray
  b2: np.ndarray
  name: str = "mlp"

  def __call__(self, x, *, mask=None, scale=1.0):
    if isinstance(x, RaggedArray):
      h = np.tanh(x.values @ self.w1 + self.b1)
      y = (h @ self.w2 + self.b2) * scale
      return RaggedArray(y, x.offsets)
    h = np.tanh(x @ self.w1 + self.b1)
    y = (h @ self.w2 + self.b2) * scale
    if mask is not None:
      y = np.where(mask[:, None], y, np.float32(0.0))
    return y


def apply_with_kwargs(fn, x, *args, **kwargs):
  return fn(x, *args, **kwargs)


@par.jit
def score_structure(backbone, features, block, neg_gamma, mask=None):
  bb = backbone.centered()
  msgs = bb.rbf_message_passing(features, neg_gamma)
  step = functools.partial(apply_with_kwargs, block, scale=np.float32(0.5))
  out = step(msgs, mask=mask)
  match out:
    case RaggedArray(values=vals):
      return par.reduce(operator.add, vals * vals)
    case _:
      return np.sum(out * out)

docs.text:

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Python function + argument types
        │  elaborate (parakeet/frontend/, lib/)
        ▼
 operator IR (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, IndexScatter)
        │  middle-end passes + lowering (parakeet/transforms/)  ──►  f.specialize(x).operators / .ir
        ▼
 typed loop IR (parakeet/syntax/ir.py)
        │  emit C (backends/c.py)            ├─► Metal kernels (backends/metal.py)
        ▼                                    └─► CUDA kernels  (backends/cuda.py)
 system C compiler ─► shared library, cached on disk ─► called through ctypes

docs.title: Specialization
docs.text: Calling a @jit function classifies its arguments; dtype, rank, and layout of arrays, the types of scalars, the structure of tuples/records, and the identity of functions; into a type key. Each distinct key gets one compiled specialization, cached per function. Values read from globals and closures are classified the same way on every call and passed as hidden arguments, so compiled code never sees stale data.

docs.title: Elaboration
docs.text:
The frontend is a staged interpreter: it walks the function's Python AST with an environment of compile-time values and emits IR only for what must happen at run time.

  • Scalars are IR expressions with a NumPy type.
  • Tuples, NamedTuples, fixed-key dicts, frozen dataclasses, slices, functions, closures, and dtypes exist at compile time. Calling a helper function means elaborating its body in place, so by the time IR is produced there are no Python calls, closures, or tuple objects left.
  • Arrays are either concrete (a buffer plus offset, shape, and strides as scalar expressions; slicing is just arithmetic on those) or delayed: a function from index to element. np.tanh(x * a) + b builds a delayed array three layers deep, and no operator is emitted until something consumes it: a store, a reduction, or return. That consumer's operator evaluates the whole expression per element. This handles basic element-wise fusion by construction; larger multi-operator rewrites happen next in the middle end.

Three questions cannot be answered in one forward pass, so elaboration is restarted with what it learned:

  1. the type of a variable modified in a loop (x = 0 then x += 0.5; restart with x: float);
  2. whether a delayed array must be evaluated eagerly; because it would be evaluated twice, inside a loop, or after an array it reads has been modified (which would change the answer);
  3. which arguments must be compile-time constants (axis=axis), in which case the specialization is additionally keyed on that argument's value.

docs.title: The operator IR
docs.text:
The result of elaboration is a small imperative language: typed scalar variables, flat buffers with load/store, if, counted and unbounded loops, scoped buffer allocation, and runtime checks. On top of it sit five core operator statements, preserving the adverb algebra of the original NYU compiler:

  • IndexMap(shape, index, body): run body for every index; iterations are independent.
  • IndexReduce(shape, index, body, folds): fold the values body computes at every index; each Fold stores its combiner block, an associative primitive name when recognized, and optional multi-state carries. With where, only indices satisfying a predicate participate.
  • IndexFilter(n, index, body, keep): compact the indices where keep holds, in order, into a new array.
  • IndexScan(n, index, body, fold, emit): a running fold; emit runs at every index with the running state.
  • IndexScatter(shape, index, body, dest_size, target, updates): associative index-directed scatter-add (np.bincount, parakeet.scatter_add), supporting multiple fused updates over a shared key.

Tiling passes introduce IndexTile and TileStage nodes on top of the same IR. spec.operators prints a function before the middle-end passes, and spec.ir prints it after lowering. The final pass (transforms/lowering.py) replaces operator statements with loops and with the single parallel construct, ParLoop, which runs its body over chunks of an index range.

Memory management is static: a buffer belongs to the scope that allocated it and is released when that scope ends, unless it escapes into a longer-lived variable, in which case a reference count keeps it alive. Parallel loop bodies never mutate reference counts of shared buffers.

docs.title: Middle-end passes
docs.text:
parakeet/transforms/pipeline.py lists the eleven passes over the operator statements in order (parakeet.transforms.pipeline.names()). Every pass is checked by parakeet.verify when config.verify is enabled, and config.skip_transforms can omit individual passes:

  1. Dead code (simplify.py): removes pure operator statements and unused allocations that nothing reads, to a fixed point.
  2. Normalize (normalize.py): squeezes unit keepdims=True map axes and hoists row-invariant inner reductions (softmax, layer_norm).
  3. Vertical fusion (fusion.py): collapses producer-consumer operator pairs (Map → Map including affine transposes/slices and matmul epilogues, Scan → Map into IndexScan.emit, Map → Filter, Map → Reduce, Map → Scatter) and flattens nested maps.
  4. Filter fusion (fusion.py): merges adjacent IndexFilters into one short-circuiting filter and turns Filter → Reduce into a zero-allocation guarded IndexReduce.
  5. Sibling fusion (fusion.py): merges independent IndexReduces, pure IndexMaps, compatible IndexScatters sharing a key, and online max + sum(exp(x - m)) pairs into single passes.
  6. Contraction reassociation (reassociate.py): reorders chained bilinear contractions when doing so saves FLOPs (including latent-attention absorption).
  7. Monoidal tiling (monoid_tile.py): tiles rescaled semiring reductions (attention, Split-K decoding, linear cross-entropy, Gaussian regression) and applies affine tile-interval mask pruning.
  8. Chunkwise scan (tile_scan.py): rewrites affine and bilinear matrix-state for recurrences into parallel chunkwise scans.
  9. Pairwise fold tiling (pairwise_fold.py): fuses pairwise score producers into ordered tile-summary folds on CPU and GPU (such as exact 1-NN).
  10. Reduction interchange (tiling.py): hoists strided commutative, associative inner reductions outside L1-sized contiguous output strips on CPU (PermuteReductions).
  11. Tiling (tiling.py): rewrites maps wrapping reductions into nested cache/register tiles on CPU and shared-memory tiles on CUDA and Metal.

After those eleven passes, lowering (lowering.py) turns operators into loops and ParLoop chunks.

One transform still runs during elaboration rather than as a middle-end pass:

  • Differentiation (autodiff.py, derivatives.py, algebraic_vjp.py): grad elaborates the function with a tape that records array operators on differentiated values, runs algebraic rematerialization rules (for attention, cross-entropy, and norms), and walks the tape backwards to emit adjoint operators. Scalars differentiate directly from their expression trees, and views map to the same views of their adjoint buffers.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
All targets are C-like, so one emitter (backends/cfamily.py) prints scalar expressions and control flow while backend modules supply target types, math intrinsics, tiled GPU codegen (backends/tiled_gpu.py, backends/monoidal_gpu.py), and runtime error reporting.

  • The host program is always C. Each ParLoop body is outlined into a function taking a context struct (identical bodies up to alpha-renaming share one compiled function) and dispatched through a function pointer supplied at call time (the thread pool, OpenMP, GCD, or a sequential loop) so one compiled library serves every CPU backend.
  • For GPU backends, eligible ParLoops and tiled plans are also emitted as Metal or CUDA kernels. Arrays stay resident on the device across consecutive GPU kernels within a call (and across calls when wrapped with parakeet.to_device).

Scalar helpers (Python/NumPy floor division and modulo, integer powers, shifts, NaN-propagating min/max, and the RNG) live once as C text and are included in the C, Metal, and CUDA preludes so all backends agree bit-for-bit on integer results.

docs.title: Calling convention
docs.text: A compiled entry point takes flat arrays of 64-bit slots: scalars, and for each array its buffer pointer, offset, shape, and strides. Results return the same way. Buffers allocated by compiled code are handed to NumPy without copying using a finalizer that releases the native reference; views of inputs return as NumPy views of the caller's memory.

docs.title: The compiled language
docs.text: Parakeet compiles a subset of Python chosen so that every value has a type known at compile time. This page describes that subset and the places where compiled code deliberately differs from running the same function in CPython.

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
Python value Inside compiled code int, float, bool 64-bit integer / double / bool, weakly typed like NumPy treats Python scalars NumPy scalars (np.float32(1), np.complex64(1+2j), ...) scalars of exactly that dtype (complex lowers to unboxed (re, im) float pairs) NumPy arrays bool, int8–int64, uint8–uint64, float32, float64, complex64, complex128; any number of dimensions, any strides tuples (also nested) compile-time structures of the above NamedTuples and @dataclass objects (frozen or non-frozen) fields hold scalar, array, or nested record leaves; supports pure methods, @property, __call__, and local functional field rebinding (obj.x = v) dictionaries with fixed string keys key order is part of the structure, with lookup by literal key lists, list comprehensions homogeneous numeric literals build arrays; [] and mutated/heterogeneous lists compile as zero-overhead compile-time lists (.append, .extend, .pop, .clear), automatically promoting to a growable CPU buffer when mutated inside a dynamic loop or runtime branch; use par.fixed_list(cap, dtype) for zero-malloc thread-local scratch inside parallel loops and GPU kernels None, strings, dtypes, functions, modules compile-time constants slice, range, zip, enumerate, itertools (pairwise, islice, chain, product, batched) supported as values and in zero-allocation for loops / generator expressions

float16 data is widened to float32. complex64 and complex128 lower to unboxed (re, im) float views across CPU, multicore, Apple Metal (complex64), and CUDA, and compose with Wirtinger par.grad and par.jvp. Object arrays, general-purpose mutable containers, sets and arbitrary non-dataclass class instances are not supported; passing one raises a TypeError naming the type.

Type promotion follows NumPy 2 (NEP 50) exactly: float32_array * 2.0 stays float32, int8_array + 1 stays int8, int32_array / 2 is float64.

docs.title: Statements
docs.text:
Supported: assignment (including tuple unpacking, augmented and annotated assignment, :=), if/elif/else, for over ranges, arrays, tuples, zip and enumerate, optional else on for and while, break, continue, return anywhere, nested def and lambda, assert, raise of built-in exceptions with a literal message, pass, del.

Not supported: try/except, with, classes, generators (yield), global /nonlocal, import inside a compiled function, f-strings and print. Each of these produces an UnsupportedError at the offending line.

Loop else runs on normal exhaustion, including an empty input. A break skips the corresponding else suite. Strict zip checks lengths at exhaustion. Chained scalar comparisons evaluate each reached operand once and short-circuit.

Unfiltered multi-for comprehensions over independent ranges or arrays compile as Cartesian maps. The rightmost iterator varies fastest. A scalar consumer such as sum(x * y for x in xs for y in ys) can fuse the map into its reduction. Inner iterators with observable setup and dependent domains such as for j in range(i) are outside this subset.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• Any Python function called from compiled code is inlined: helpers do not need @jit. Recursion is therefore not possible and is reported as an error.
  • Positional, keyword, default, keyword-only, *args, and **kwargs arguments (as well as **d unpacking from compile-time dicts, functools.partial, and operator.* callables) all work cleanly.
  • Functions are first-class at compile time: pass them as arguments, store them in variables, close over local variables.
  • Globals and closure variables are read on every call, like in Python. If a global changes type, a new specialization is compiled.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Compiled code follows NumPy semantics for views and mutation:

@jit
def f(x):
  v = x[1:]  # a view of the caller's array
  v[0] = 0  # ... so this modifies x
  x += 1  # in place, visible to the caller
  y = x * 2  # a new array
  x[1:] = x[:-1]  # overlapping assignment behaves as if a temporary were made
  return y
  • Basic indexing (x[i, 1:-1, ::2, None, ...]), integer-array indexing and boolean masks work for reading and writing.
  • Indices are bounds-checked (IndexError); shapes are checked when broadcasting (ValueError). Use @jit(bounds_check=False) to drop index checks.
  • Returning an input returns the same object; returning a view of an input returns a NumPy view of the caller's memory.
  • Read-only arrays may be read; writing to one raises ValueError.

docs.title: Differences from CPython / NumPy
docs.text:
One static type per variable : A variable assigned an int on one path and a float on another is a float everywhere (the usual numeric promotion). A function returning 1 in one branch and 2.5 in another returns a float from both. Types that cannot be unified (say an array and None) are an error if the variable is used afterwards.

Rank is static : The number of dimensions of every array is fixed at compile time. Functions whose result rank depends on values (for example np.squeeze(x) when it cannot be known which dimensions have length 1) ask you to pass axis=.

Compile-time constants : Some arguments must be known at compile time: axis, keepdims, the length of a shape tuple, a dtype. If such a value comes straight from an argument of the compiled function, Parakeet specialises on its value automatically; otherwise it reports which expression must be constant.

Lists and dynamic loops : Numeric literals like [1.0, 2.0, 3.0] and [f(x) for x in xs] still build arrays directly. Local lists built with outs = []; outs.append(...) stay completely unboxed at compile time in straight-line and unrolled code (so np.stack(outs) and RaggedArray.from_sequences(outs) work with zero heap allocation and compose with par.grad), and automatically promote to a growable homogeneous CPU buffer with geometric doubling when appended inside a runtime for/while loop or dynamic if branch. Inside parallel par.parfor/par.map bodies and GPU kernels (CUDA/Metal), par.fixed_list(cap, dtype) provides a fixed-capacity stack-allocated scratch buffer with zero malloc. Variables holding arrays or RaggedArrays may also be rebound to different shapes across while/for loop iterations (for example, shrinking an active frontier with arr = arr[mask]).

Integer arithmetic : Python ints are 64-bit and wrap on overflow (like NumPy), they are not arbitrary precision.

float16 : Operations NumPy would compute in half precision are computed in float32.

Loop variables after a loop : A variable first assigned inside a loop body keeps its last value after the loop, but if the loop never ran it is zero (CPython raises NameError).

Random numbers : np.random functions use Parakeet's own generator (see parakeet.seed); the streams differ from NumPy's.

Parallel side effects : parakeet.map, comprehensions and array expressions may evaluate their elements in parallel and in any order. Reductions with a user-defined function assume it is associative only when Parakeet can prove it (for +, *, min, max, &, |, ^); otherwise they run sequentially.

docs.title: Fixed records at the call boundary
docs.text: Named tuples preserve their field names and result type. @dataclass objects (frozen or non-frozen) and dictionaries with fixed string keys can contain arrays, scalars, discrete metadata, or nested records. Pure methods, @property, @staticmethod, @classmethod, and __call__ on dataclasses and named tuples are inlined directly at elaboration time with zero PyObject overhead, and local field assignments (obj.x = v, obj.x += v) on non-frozen dataclasses functionally rebind the compile-time record (value semantics, zero heap mutation). Fields and keys are part of the specialization, while array data and scalar fields remain ordinary runtime arguments. Returning these containers reconstructs their structure and keeps the usual array view semantics.

docs.title: Migrating from Parakeet 0.x
docs.text:
Parakeet 1.0 is a rewrite for Python 3.11+. The decorator and the operators keep their names, and most 0.x programs run after the usual Python 2 → 3 changes (xrange → range, / → // for integer division, print(...)).

0.x 1.0 Python 2.7, dsltools, appdirs Python 3.11+, NumPy 2, nothing else config.backend = "openmp" still works; default is "auto", which needs no OpenMP "llvm" backend removed "interp" backend "python" (runs the original function) "cuda" via PyCUDA + nvcc "cuda" via CuPy, no toolkit install; new "metal" backend f(x, _backend="c") unchanged; also @jit(backend="c") @macro still there, with a different contract: the function gets the compiler and the compile-time values of its arguments instead of syntax nodes (this is how map, reduce and the NumPy functions are defined). @typed_macro and @staged_macro are gone; arguments such as axis are specialised automatically parakeet.testing_helpers parakeet.testing (the old name still imports) config.opt_fusion, config.print_specialized_function, config.print_generated_code still accepted, as aliases of fusion, print_ir and print_code; the other opt_* flags are gone (see Configuration) parakeet.prims.add, parakeet.ndtypes.Int64, Float64, ... unchanged tuple parameters def f((a, b)) not valid Python 3; unpack in the body typed_repr(f, args), specialize(f, args), run_python_fn(f, args) unchanged (also f.specialize(*args).ir) find_broken_transform(fn, inputs, expected) unchanged in spirit: it switches fusion, tiling, the C optimizer and parallel loops on one at a time and names the first that changes the result parakeet.frontend, parakeet.syntax, parakeet.transforms, parakeet.lib the same packages, with new contents: the staged interpreter, the loop IR, and tiling / differentiation parakeet.rank, size, shape, erf, norm, ... unchanged

docs.title: Behaviour changes
docs.text:
• Result types follow NumPy 2. In 0.x bool + bool gave an integer and integer power gave a float; now both give what NumPy gives. Python scalars no longer upcast float32 arrays.
  • Bounds are checked by default. Programs that silently read out of bounds under 0.x now raise IndexError.
  • np.array(x) copies, x += 1 updates in place, views alias: as in NumPy.
  • Globals are read at call time rather than captured at first compilation.
  • parakeet.reduce is parallel only for combiners known to be associative; 0.x assumed associativity for any function.
  • imap(f, shape) passes f a tuple whenever shape is a tuple, including one-element tuples.

docs.title: Data-parallel operators
docs.text:
Parakeet exposes one unified operator surface on the top-level parakeet module. Every operator below works both inside @parakeet.jit (where it fuses into surrounding NumPy code) and directly from ordinary Python (automatically JIT-compiling any callable arguments):

import numpy as np
import parakeet as par
Operator Meaning par.map(f, x, y, ..., axis=0) f applied to corresponding slices along axis; axis=None applies it to every scalar element par.allpairs(f, x, y, axis=0) result[i, j] = f(x[i], y[j]) par.outer_map(f, x, y, z, ...) the n-ary generalisation of allpairs par.reduce(f, x, ..., init=None, axis=None, map=None) fold f over all elements, or over slices along axis; with map=g and several arrays, over g(x[i], y[i], ...) par.fold(lift, merge, x, init=None, *, axis=None, indexed=False, emit=None) associative structured fold over tuple / NamedTuple states (tiles pairwise folds automatically) par.scan(f, x, ..., init=None, axis=0, map=None, emit=None) running fold (a generalised cumsum); emit=h gives h of each running value par.imap(f, shape) result[i, j, ...] = f(i, j, ...) for every index of shape (unpacks multi-axis indices automatically; 1-arg tuple lambda ij: also works) par.ireduce(f, shape, init=None, combine=np.add) reduce f(i, ...) over every index of shape par.parfor(f, shape) call f(i, ...) for its side effects, in parallel par.filter(pred, x, ..., map=None) the elements of x for which pred is true; with several arrays, map(x[i], y[i], ...) where pred(x[i], y[i], ...) holds par.filter_reduce(f, pred, x, ..., map=None, init=None, axis=None) reduce with f over elements where pred holds (fuses into one zero-allocation guarded reduction loop when init is given) par.flatmap(count_fn, emit_fn, n) / par.filter_pairs(...) two-pass 1-to-K ragged compaction (IndexExpand) par.split_bytes(buf, sep=10, skip_empty=False) / par.parse_int64 / par.parse_float32 / par.parse_float64 zero-PyObject delimiter splitting into RaggedArray[uint8] and compiled ASCII integer/float parsing over uint8 slices or RaggedArray[uint8] par.fixed_list(capacity, dtype=np.float32) fixed-capacity, zero-malloc thread-local scratch list (.append, .pop, .clear, indexing, len) for stacks and per-thread buffers inside par.parfor / par.map on CPU, CUDA, and Metal par.scatter_add(n, idx, vals, where=None) / par.scatter_add(n, ((k, v) for ...)) index-directed associative scatter-add (IndexScatter) with thread-privatized parallel lowering and exact gather adjoint (also targeted automatically by np.bincount, np.add.at, canonical for i: out[idx[i]] += vals[i] loops, and filtered comprehensions like [np.sum(vals[idx == b]) for b in range(n)]) par.wavefront(...) / par.batched_wavefront(...) / par.soft_align(...) 2D and banded semiring dynamic programming (IndexWavefront) with checkpointed VJP par.grad, par.value_and_grad, par.jvp, par.vjp, par.hvp, par.linearize, par.linear_transpose, par.jacfwd, par.jacrev, par.hessian composable reverse-mode, forward-mode, and higher-order AD; see Automatic differentiation par.show_rewrite(f, *args) inspect which algebraic optimizations rewrote f and view before/after IR; see Algebraic laws 
par.map(lambda row: row / np.sum(row), X)  # normalise rows
par.allpairs(lambda a, b: np.sum((a - b) ** np.float32(2)), X, C)  # distance matrix
par.reduce(np.maximum, X, axis=0)  # column maxima
par.imap(lambda i, j: i * 10 + j, (3, 4))  # an index-defined 2D array

par.reduce(np.add, x, y, map=np.multiply)  # a dot product; no array of products is built
par.scan(np.add, x, y, map=lambda a, b: a - b)  # running sum of differences
par.filter(lambda a, b: a > b, x, y, map=np.add)  # x + y where x > y

For multi-dimensional shapes, imap, ireduce, and parfor unpack coordinates directly when the function takes len(shape) parameters (lambda i, j: ...), and still accept a single index tuple (lambda ij: ...) for backward compatibility. parakeet.dsl remains available as a compatibility alias re-exporting these same operators alongside compact dtype shorthands (dsl.f32, dsl.i64).

docs.title: Functions that return arrays
docs.text:
The function given to map may return an array; the results are stacked.

par.map(lambda row: np.cumsum(row), X)  # shape (n, m)

All results must have the same shape; this is checked at run time (ValueError).

docs.title: Parallelism and associativity
docs.text: map-like operators evaluate elements in parallel, in no particular order. reduce runs in parallel when the combining function is recognisably one of +, *, min, max, and, or, &, |, ^ (whether written as np.add, lambda a, b: a + b, or par.add), and sequentially otherwise; so a non-associative function such as lambda acc, x: acc * 0.5 + x still gives the same answer as functools.reduce. Floating-point sums are reassociated, like NumPy's own pairwise summation: expect differences in the last digits.

docs.title: Primitive combiner functions
docs.text: Standard NumPy ufuncs (np.add, np.subtract, np.multiply, np.divide, np.minimum, np.maximum) are the idiomatic combiners to pass to par.reduce, par.ireduce, par.scan, and par.filter. Parakeet also exports matching aliases (par.add, par.minimum, etc.) for backward compatibility.

docs.title: Structured reductions
docs.text:
par.fold(lift, merge, x, init) lifts each axis-0 slice of x to a nonempty tuple or named tuple of scalar fields. The pure merge(left, right) must be associative and return the same field types. Chunks may regroup adjacent values while preserving input order. The initial state is applied once, and is the result for empty input. Read any field of the result in compiled code.

For example, affine updates s -> a*s + b compose in order with merge(left, right) = (right[0]*left[0], right[0]*left[1] + right[1]). Custom folds support forward evaluation. The initial state is optional. With no seed, the first lifted element starts the fold and evaluating an empty lane raises ValueError.

Use axis=k to fold the scalar values along each lane of a multidimensional array. Pass emit=project to return a scalar per lane. With indexed=True, lift(value, index) receives the zero-based position on that axis. The projection runs after the final merge, including on the seed for an empty lane. The gallery composes this operation with allpairs and uses the same score with two different merge rules.

docs.title: Tiled pairwise folds
docs.text:
On CPU, a map over queries can consume an associative structured fold over references whose inputs come from a feature reduction. For example, both the gallery's nested-map 1-NN and the following NumPy expression compile to the same tiled computation:

@par.jit
def nearest(x, y):
  return np.argmin(np.sum((x[:, None, :] - y[None, :, :]) ** np.float32(2), axis=2), axis=1)

The compiler evaluates a bounded rectangle of scores, folds each row, and merges consecutive tile summaries in reference order. Each summary carries the global reference index, so ties and NaNs retain their first-index semantics across tiles. The same rewrite handles other pure score reductions, including a sum of absolute differences followed by argmax. The rewrite inspector reports Pairwise map and ordered tile-summary fold when it applies.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Looking for cross-library benchmarks?

For head-to-head 1.0 comparisons against PyTorch, JAX, CuPy, Faiss, and PyKeOps on CPU and an NVIDIA A10, see Release benchmarks. This page explains when and why Parakeet wins or loses on CPUs and GPUs, how cache tiling behaves, and practical tuning tips.

All numbers on this page were measured with python benchmarks/run.py on an Apple M1 Pro (10 cores, 32 GB), macOS 26.5, Python 3.12.6, NumPy 2.5.5; best of five runs, compilation excluded. "NumPy" is the same computation written with NumPy alone; "×" is the speed-up over it. Run the script on your own machine - results vary a lot between CPUs, compilers and array sizes.

docs.title: A big GPU on the work it is for
docs.text:
python benchmarks/gpu_showcase.py on an NVIDIA A100 (Google Colab, 12 CPU threads, float32). The same Python source runs in every column.

kernel size NumPy one core 12 threads A100 A100 vs 12 threads n-body forces 16,384 bodies – 1393 ms 238 ms 7.5 ms 32× k-means assignment 2M points × 256 centers × 16 2247 ms 9551 ms 1913 ms 75.8 ms 25× heat equation, 200 steps 2048² 7821 ms 4532 ms 370 ms 118 ms 3.1× Black-Scholes 20M options 625 ms 1746 ms 227 ms 111 ms 2.0× Julia set 4096² – 1425 ms 155 ms 95.5 ms 1.6×

The first two are what a GPU is for: every element needs thousands of operations and the result is small. The n-body kernel is 186× faster than one core. The last three are bounded by moving their arrays across the bus once each way (Black-Scholes reads 240 MB and writes 80 MB); the heat equation is 600 loops over a grid that never leaves the device between them, which before arrays stayed on the device took 1.4 s here.

A float matrix product is not in this table: on the CPU it goes to the BLAS (24 ms for 2048² on this machine), on the GPU it is Parakeet's own kernel (73 ms). Dense linear algebra on a GPU wants cuBLAS, which Parakeet does not call.

docs.title: Where the GPU starts to win
docs.text:
python benchmarks/crossover.py times the same kernel across sizes. On the same kind of machine (Tesla T4, 2 CPU threads, float32), after tiling and with gradients:

kernel size NumPy one core 2 threads CUDA np.tanh(x * a) + b 100k 0.18 ms 3.3 ms 2.6 ms 0.77 ms 1M 1.7 ms 29.9 ms 30.6 ms 2.8 ms 10M 39.0 ms 277 ms 164 ms 75.5 ms all-pairs distances 1k × 64 9.3 ms 0.42 ms 0.41 ms 0.77 ms 100k × 64 760 ms 34.5 ms 27.3 ms 42.5 ms matrix product 512² 2.5 ms 10.1 ms 8.0 ms 14.3 ms 1024² 24.8 ms 62.3 ms 63.1 ms 49.6 ms 2048² 145 ms 510 ms 654 ms 375 ms Julia set 256² – 5.2 ms 3.0 ms 0.81 ms 1024² – 82.2 ms 47.0 ms 6.4 ms 2048² – 338 ms 197 ms 78.2 ms Harris corners 1024² 9.7 ms 2.9 ms 4.0 ms 3.0 ms 4096² 292 ms 77.0 ms 88.8 ms 133 ms MLP gradient (784-256-10) batch 64 – 3.7 ms 4.1 ms 5.5 ms batch 4096 – 231 ms 189 ms 139 ms decision tree fit (32 features) 100k rows – 4.2 s 3.0 s 2.9 s (CPU)

The GPU wins once each element costs real arithmetic (the Julia set from the smallest size, tanh from about 100k elements) and the result is not much bigger than the work that produced it. It ties or loses when a loop mostly moves memory, because every launch pays for the copy both ways: Harris at 4096² and all-pairs at 100k rows are slower on the device than on two CPU threads. Loops below config.device_threshold (32,768 iterations) never leave the CPU, which is why the decision tree, whose parallel loops run over 32 features, is a CPU program on every backend.

The matrix product is the tiled one: on this machine it is within 2.5–3.5× of NumPy's OpenBLAS on one core.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
Where Parakeet wins. Expressions with several operations (no temporaries, one pass over memory), code that needs a Python-level loop in NumPy (Julia set, GrowCut, pairwise kernels), and anything that can use all cores.

Where it does not.

  • Dense linear algebra, when there is no BLAS to call. A product of two float matrices is handed to the BLAS NumPy itself uses, so it costs what it costs in NumPy. Parakeet's own tiled loops run everything else that has that shape (integer products, allpairs distances, products inside a parallel map or on a GPU) and are 3–10× behind a hand-tuned BLAS.
  • Single-threaded transcendental functions. NumPy ships SIMD implementations of tanh, sin, exp, ...; Parakeet's sequential backend calls the C math library one element at a time (the tanh row). With threads it is ahead again.
  • Memory-bound loops on a GPU. On this machine the 10 CPU cores usually beat the integrated GPU unless each element needs a lot of arithmetic (arc distance, convolution). Loops that mostly move memory (norm, stencils) lose, and repeatedly launching cheap kernels over a NumPy-owned array (diffusion) loses badly because the array is copied to and from the device on every launch.
  • Tiny inputs. A call into compiled code costs a few microseconds of argument marshalling; a NumPy call on a 10-element array is cheaper.

docs.title: Tiling
docs.text:
A matmul-shaped operation is a map over pairs whose element is a reduction over data picked by each member of the pair: a matrix product, allpairs distances, a tropical product. Evaluated row by row, every row of the result sweeps over all of the second operand, which stops fitting in cache long before the arrays are large. Parakeet recognises the shape; any two-dimensional map whose element function is one reduction plus straight-line code, whoever wrote it; and does two things:

  • tiles the inner dimension, so a cache-sized block of the second operand is reused for every row before moving on (config.tile_bytes, by default half of a core's L2 cache);
  • jams the reductions of a 2×4 block of elements into one loop, so each loaded value is used several times.

Neither changes what is computed, only the order. a @ b on 1024×1024 float64 (Apple M1 Max):

one core all cores untiled 190 ms 43 ms tiled 92 ms 13 ms NumPy (Accelerate) 4.5 ms

@jit(tiling=False) or config.tiling = False turns it off. The timings above are with config.blas = False; by default a float matrix product on a CPU backend calls the BLAS and takes the NumPy time.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Prefer array expressions or comprehensions over index loops when they say the same thing: they parallelise, explicit for loops do not.
  • Keep work inside one @jit function so expressions can fuse across helper calls (helpers are inlined automatically).
  • @jit(bounds_check=False) removes index checks from explicit indexing in loops once the code is known to be correct.
  • Compiled code is specialised on whether an input is C-contiguous; contiguous arrays give the C compiler unit strides to vectorise.
  • parakeet.config.fast_math = True allows the C compiler to reorder floating-point arithmetic everywhere (results may change in the last digits).

docs.title: 1. Specialize on types and shapes at call time
docs.text:
Python is dynamically typed, yet numerical functions are almost always called with the same dtypes and ranks at a given call site. Parakeet treats your Python function as a template and compiles a native specialization for each distinct combination of argument dtypes, array ranks, memory layouts (contiguous vs. strided), and container structure.

When an expression's type or rank depends on a value; such as axis=, a tuple length, or a unit dimension of length 1 that controls broadcasting; Parakeet specializes on that value automatically. That resolves the broadcasting corner case noted in Rubinsteyn's thesis (200×1 + 1×300) statically at compile time.

docs.title: 2. Lower everything to a small index-operator core
docs.text:
Instead of maintaining hundreds of hand-written C or GPU kernels for every NumPy function, Parakeet defines array expressions, comprehensions, matrix products, einsum, and user-written adverbs in terms of a small set of core index-operator statements:

  • IndexMap: independent computation over an index space
  • IndexReduce: associative or sequential folds (including multi-carry state such as argmin/argmax and online logsumexp, plus guarded filtered reductions)
  • IndexScan: prefix folds with an optional emit stage
  • IndexFilter: 1-to-0/1 stream compaction of indices matching a predicate
  • IndexExpand: 1-to-K ragged compaction (flatmap, filter_pairs)
  • IndexScatter: associative index-directed scatter-add (np.bincount, parakeet.scatter_add)
  • IndexWavefront: anti-diagonal / banded 2D semiring dynamic programming (wavefront, batched_wavefront, soft_align)
  • IndexTile: explicit cache and GPU shared-memory tile staging emitted by the middle end

You can inspect a function at this level at any time via f.specialize(*args).operators or parakeet.show_rewrite(f, *args).

docs.title: 3. Fuse algebraically before lowering to loops
docs.text:
Because programs stay in this small operator IR until the end of the pipeline, optimizations are algebraic identities rather than fragile loop-nest analyses:

  • Vertical fusion collapses producer-consumer chains: map into map (including transposes, slices, stencils, and matmul epilogues like np.tanh(a @ b + c)), map into reduce/scan/filter/scatter, map after scan, filter into filter, and filter into reduce (turning np.sum(x[x > 0]) into one zero-allocation loop).
  • Nested map flattening turns a map inside a map into one multi-dimensional IndexMap, exposing the full index space to CPU threads and GPU grids.
  • Sibling and online fusion lets independent consumers over the same index space share a pass (x.min(), x.max(), np.sin(x), np.cos(x), or sibling histograms with the same bin IDs) and merges dependent max + sum(exp(x - m)) pairs into a single associative pass.
  • Dead-operator elimination drops pure operators and allocations that nothing reads before loops are emitted.

Parakeet 1.0 adds the safety conditions the 2014 thesis omitted: cost and single-use guards so fusion never silently duplicates expensive work, alias checks, and explicit associativity checks so non-associative user folds stay strictly left-to-right.

docs.title: 4. Tile for cache and GPU shared memory from the same IR
docs.text:
Following Hielscher's 2013 thesis, locality transformations operate directly on the operator statements before loop lowering:

  • Reduction interchange hoists strided inner reductions (such as np.sum(X, axis=0)) outside L1-sized strips of contiguous output columns on CPU, while leaving them coalesced across threads on GPU.
  • Invariant hoisting squeezes unit keepdims=True axes and lifts row-level reductions so normalizations like softmax and layer_norm stay L1-resident.
  • Cache, register, and GPU SRAM tiling rewrites maps wrapping reductions (a @ b, allpairs, einsum, tropical products, and fused prologues or epilogues) into nested cache and register tiles on CPU and cooperatively staged shared-memory tiles on CUDA and Metal. On Apple Silicon Metal, float32 contractions use simdgroup_matrix automatically; on CUDA sm_80+, config.tensor_cores=True enables nvcuda::wmma TF32 Tensor Cores.
  • Algebraic laws for modern reductions extend the exact same tiling machinery to rescaled semiring monoids (online softmax, Gaussian kernel regression, attention, cut cross-entropy), contraction reassociation, chunkwise affine/bilinear scans, and tile-interval mask pruning. See Algebraic laws.
  • Persistent GPU residency (parakeet.to_device / to_host) keeps arrays and parameter tuples on CUDA or Metal across calls without repeated host copies.

docs.title: 5. Inspectable, fail-loud compilation
docs.text:
• parakeet.verify checks scoping, types, and buffer ownership before passes, after every pass, and after lowering.
  • f.specialize(*args) exposes .operators, .ir, .source, and .kernels.
  • par.show_rewrite(f, *args) summarizes which algebraic optimizations fired.
  • parakeet.find_broken_transform bisects the middle-end passes one by one.
  • Unsupported Python or NumPy features fail at compile time with the exact source caret and inlined call chain instead of silently falling back.

docs.title: What does not work yet
docs.text: Parakeet is a numerical compiler, not a drop-in replacement for all of CPython or SciPy. Knowing the boundary up front avoids surprises.

docs.title: NumPy and SciPy coverage
docs.text:
About 200 core NumPy functions and ufuncs are built in (see Supported functions), covering arithmetic, reductions, scans, sorting, masks and fancy indexing, @/dot/einsum, np.linalg.norm, and parallel np.random. Not yet built in:

  • Matrix decompositions and solvers (np.linalg.svd, solve, inv, eig, cholesky, qr, det, lstsq)
  • Spectral transforms (np.fft.*)
  • Variable-cardinality set operations (np.unique, np.lexsort, np.isin)
  • SciPy modules (scipy.special, scipy.optimize, scipy.ndimage, ...)

docs.title: Automatic differentiation (grad, jvp, vjp, hvp)
docs.text:
Parakeet provides reverse-mode (par.grad, par.value_and_grad, general non-scalar par.vjp), forward-mode (par.jvp, par.linearize), linear transposes (par.linear_transpose), and higher-order differentiation (par.hvp, par.jacfwd, par.jacrev, par.hessian) across element-wise operations, reductions (sum, zero-safe prod, min, max, general folds), cumsum and general par.scan, sort and topk, FrozenHashTable.get and SortedIndex.get, @, einsum, views and concatenation, gather and scatter (np.add.at, canonical for-loop scatter-add, par.scatter_add), map/allpairs with user functions, pure runtime if branches, and checkpointed for/while loops; enough to train transformers (examples/nanogpt.py) and convnets (examples/convnet.py). Current boundaries:

  • Elaboration-time tape & symbolic JVP: reverse-mode differentiation records operators on a tape during elaboration (with an algebraic tape optimizer for zero-$O(T^2)$ attention VJP/HVP, linear cross-entropy, softmax, and norms) rather than running as a separate IR-to-IR pass over lowered loops.
  • Loops over differentiated values: small static for loops (<= 32) unroll for cross-iteration fusion; runtime-bound and long for loops use IR-level O(sqrt(T)) checkpointed reverse loops; data-dependent while loops use fixed-slot stride-doubling checkpointing; forward-mode jvp streams tangents in O(1) memory; and par.checkpoint, par.stop_gradient, @par.custom_vjp, and @par.custom_jvp provide explicit control over rematerialization and custom/implicit rules. Loops with break/continue over active state remain refused loudly.
  • Pure runtime if branches in reverse mode: both branches execute and are selected by the condition, so branches touching differentiated values cannot contain array stores, return, break, or raise.
  • Missing derivative rules (refused loudly): cumprod, convolve, arbitrary indexed overwrites (out[idx] = v; use np.add.at, for i: out[idx[i]] += v, or par.scatter_add for scatter-add), and overwriting an array still needed by an earlier backward rule.
  • Higher-order derivatives: forward-over-reverse par.hvp and par.hessian compose through element-wise ops, reductions, @, views, checkpointed loops, LayerNorm, and zero-$O(T^2)$ attention; reverse-over-reverse grad(grad(...)) also supports np.stack, np.cumsum, gather indexing, scatter-add, and scalar 1-to-1 par.map, while refusing non-scalar user map bodies loudly.

docs.title: GPU and locality boundaries
docs.text:
• Apple Metal has no hardware float64: float64 loops fall back to CPU cores with a warning; use float32 on Metal.
  • No per-thread heap allocation on GPU: a parallel loop that allocates temporary arrays or selects between buffer aliases inside its body runs on CPU instead of CUDA or Metal.
  • Dense GEMM vs. cuBLAS: CPU backends call NumPy's BLAS for standalone float A @ B. GPU backends run Parakeet's own shared-memory tiled kernels (including Metal simdgroup_matrix and optional CUDA TF32 WMMA), which fuse prologues and epilogues in one kernel but trail hand-tuned cuBLAS on large standalone matrix multiplies.
  • Analytical tile sizing: tile sizes are picked analytically from target cache and shared-memory budgets (config.tile_bytes) rather than Hielscher's online runtime search. Chunkwise TileScan handles affine and bilinear recurrences; general cache-tiled TiledScan for arbitrary scans is not implemented.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Parakeet started in OCaml as an array compiler modeling the array language Q, later shifted to modeling Python, and was eventually reimplemented in Python at New York University by Alex Rubinsteyn (@iskandr), with major contributions from Eric Hielscher (@hielscher) and Nathaniel Weinman, guidance from Dennis Shasha, and advice from Russell Power. That earlier work was hosted at parakeetpython.com and documented in:

  • Alex Rubinsteyn, Runtime Compilation of Array-Oriented Python Programs (PhD thesis, NYU, 2014): type and value specialization, data-parallel adverbs, and algebraic fusion.
  • Eric Hielscher, Alex Rubinsteyn, and Dennis Shasha, Locality Optimization for Data Parallel Programs (NYU CS Technical Report TR2013-955 / Eric Hielscher's 2013 NYU PhD thesis work): TiledMap, TiledReduce, and TiledScan for unified cache tiling, register blocking, and loop interchange over adverb trees.
  • Papers and talks: HotPar '12 (Parakeet: A Just-In-Time Parallel Accelerator for Python), PyData Boston '13, and PyData NYC '13 (Python on the GPU with Parakeet).

When the Python 2 codebase was retired, its README noted that general Python is a poor fit for high-performance numerical code and that compilers work much better over a small set of explicit data-parallel operators. Parakeet 1.x is a rewrite for Python 3.11+ and NumPy 2 that keeps @jit and NumPy alongside those explicit operators, fixes the soundness gaps from the earlier design, and adds Apple Metal, NVIDIA CUDA, composable automatic differentiation, and tiled monoidal reductions.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer and NumPy 2.
  • A C compiler: the Xcode command line tools on macOS (xcode-select --install), gcc or clang on Linux, MinGW-w64 gcc or LLVM clang on Windows.

Install Parakeet in your environment (or python -m pip install . in a local checkout):

pip install parakeet
python -c "import parakeet; print(parakeet.available_backends())"

available_backends() reports, for every backend, either "ok" or the reason it cannot be used on this machine and how to fix it.

docs.title: Your first compiled function
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import parakeet as par


@par.jit
def rms(x):
  return np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x))


x = np.random.rand(1_000_000)
rms(x)  # first call: compiles for (float64 array, 1-d), then runs
rms(x)  # later calls: straight into native code
rms(x.astype(np.float32))  # a new specialization, compiled on demand

Compilation takes a few hundred milliseconds per specialization (most of it in the C compiler) and is cached on disk, so a second run of your program starts fast.

par.jit also works without decorator syntax, including on lambdas and NumPy functions:

fast_rms = par.jit(lambda x: np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x)))
par.run(rms.fn, x)  # compile-and-call in one step

docs.title: Loops, comprehensions, helpers
docs.text:
Anything in the supported subset can be mixed freely. Helper functions are inlined automatically; they do not need their own @par.jit.

def sqr_dist(a, b):
  return np.sum((a - b) ** 2)


@par.jit
def nearest(X, centroids):
  return np.array([np.argmin([sqr_dist(x, c) for c in centroids]) for x in X])

You can also call Parakeet's data-parallel operators directly (par.map, par.reduce, par.scan, par.allpairs, par.scatter_add, par.fold) when you want to apply a Python function over slices or pairs in parallel. See Data-parallel operators.

docs.title: Gradients in one line
docs.text:
Wrap any scalar-valued function with par.grad or par.value_and_grad. The forward and backward passes compile together into one native function:

def mse_loss(w, x, y):
  return np.mean((np.tanh(x @ w) - y) ** 2)


loss_val, dw = par.value_and_grad(mse_loss)(w, x, y)

See Gradients for nested parameter tuples, NamedTuples, frozen dataclasses, and training loops.

docs.title: Picking a backend
docs.text:
@par.jit(backend="metal")  # per function
def f(x): ...


f(x, _backend="c")  # per call
par.config.backend = "threads"  # process-wide
with par.options(backend="c", num_threads=1):  # temporarily
  f(x)

See Backends and GPUs for multi-core tuning, Metal, CUDA, and keeping arrays resident on a GPU with parakeet.to_device.

docs.title: Looking inside
docs.text:
spec = rms.specialize(x)  # compile without running
print(spec.operators)  # high-level operator IR before middle-end passes
print(spec.ir)  # typed, fused loop IR
print(spec.source)  # generated C

def rms(x_1: array[float64, 1d]):
    nchunks_9: int64? = @num_chunks(x_n0_3, True)
    partials_10 = alloc(float64, nchunks_9)
    parallel[reduce] for chunk_11, (start_12, stop_13) in chunks(x_n0_3, n=nchunks_9):
        x_15: float64 = (x_1[(x_off_2 + start_12)] * x_1[(x_off_2 + start_12)])
        acc_14: float64 = x_15
        for i_16 in range((start_12 + 1), stop_13, 1):  # simd
            x_17: float64 = (x_1[(x_off_2 + i_16)] * x_1[(x_off_2 + i_16)])
            acc_14: float64 = (acc_14 + x_17)
        partials_10[chunk_11] = acc_14
    acc_8: float64 = 0.0
    for i_18 in range(0, nchunks_9, 1):
        acc_8: float64 = (acc_8 + partials_10[i_18])
    red_19: float64 = acc_8
    res_20: float64 = sqrt((red_19 / float64(x_n0_3)))
    return res_20

No temporary for x * x exists: the multiplication was fused into the parallel reduction. To see a high-level summary of which algebraic rewrites fired on a function, call par.show_rewrite(fn, *example_args).summary().

docs.title: When something is not supported
docs.text:
You get a CompileError pointing at your code, not a crash:

parakeet.errors.UnsupportedError: numpy.fft.fft is not supported in compiled code
  File "demo.py", line 6, in spectrum
    return np.fft.fft(x)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Run the function uncompiled at any time with backend="python" to separate a bug in your code from a limitation of the compiler. More in Errors and debugging.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: Parakeet is benchmarked head-to-head against general array compilers (torch.compile, JAX jit, CuPy, NumPy) and specialist libraries (Faiss, PyKeOps, scikit-learn, SciPy, PyTorch SDPA / cross_entropy). Every figure plots all individual warmed replicates, the interquartile range (IQR, 25th–75th percentile), and the median directly from the committed raw JSON logs; and every workload links to its runnable source code.

docs.title: At a glance (NVIDIA L4 & 4-thread CPU)
docs.text:
Latest measurements come from one Google Colab VM with an NVIDIA L4 GPU and a 4-thread CPU at compiler revision 0dcb7d5 (float32, GPU inputs resident on device, explicit synchronization, reference-checked outputs, n = 21 GPU replicates / n = 11 CPU replicates). Download full raw JSON (samples, compile times, allocations, training logs).

Key takeaways:

  • Exact 1-NN (1,024 × 4,096 × 32): On the L4 GPU, Parakeet's ordinary broadcasting NumPy (0.223 ms) and nested-map form (0.225 ms) both beat torch.compile(cdist) (0.257 ms), PyTorch cdist (0.251 ms), JAX jit (0.500 ms), PyKeOps (0.953 ms), and CuPy (16.93 ms), trailing only Faiss GpuIndexFlatL2 (0.150 ms). On 4 CPU threads, Parakeet (7.91 ms) beats Faiss Flat (8.42 ms), PyKeOps (29.03 ms), SciPy cKDTree (54.27 ms), and NumPy (472.3 ms), just behind scikit-learn brute (6.49 ms).
  • Scaling to 16,384 references: Tiled GPU pairwise folds cut latency by 4.8× (2.597 ms → 0.542 ms on L4) and cut global scratch memory by 21× (64 MiB → 3 MiB, plus a 16 KiB shared-memory tile per block).
  • Gaussian kernel regression: On 4 CPU threads, Parakeet (42.99 ms) beats PyKeOps (66.77 ms) and NumPy (505.8 ms, 11.8× faster). On GPU, Parakeet (1.053 ms) beats PyKeOps (1.254 ms) and CuPy (17.18 ms), while torch.compile(cdist) (0.308 ms) and JAX jit (0.602 ms) lead.
  • End-to-end nanoGPT training (16 × 64 × 128 × 2): Parakeet with TF32 WMMA (6.83 ms/step) and FP32 (8.44 ms/step) both beat eager PyTorch (9.22 ms/step) with identical loss curves, while torch.compile (3.52 ms) and JAX jit (1.62 ms) lead on larger dense transformer blocks.

docs.title: End-to-end nanoGPT training (NVIDIA L4)
docs.text:
Each step runs the full forward pass, reverse-mode backpropagation, and Adam update (4 attention heads, median of 20 warmed steps in milliseconds). docs.title: Methodology notes
docs.text:
• Every benchmark arm is checked against a reference implementation (exact index equality for 1-NN and split finding; tight floating-point tolerance for reductions, attention, and training losses).
  • GPU arms time GPU-resident inputs with explicit CUDA synchronization before and after each replicate; first-call compilation times are recorded separately in the JSON downloads and excluded from warmed medians.
  • On CPU, Parakeet's pairwise fold allocates an 8 KiB (16 × 128 float32) score tile plus 192 B of row summaries per active strip; on GPU, it uses a 16 KiB shared-memory score tile per block and O(Q · #tiles) global partial winners rather than an O(Q · R) distance matrix.

docs.title: Rewrite rules and optimizations
docs.text:
Everything Parakeet does to a program between your source and the loops it runs, in one place, and how that compares with the two theses that describe the original system:

  • [R] Alex Rubinsteyn, Runtime Compilation of Array-Oriented Python Programs (NYU, 2014); the operators and their fusion rules.
  • [H] Eric Hielscher, Locality Optimization for Data Parallel Programs (NYU, 2013); tiling.

The short version: the rules are the same algebra, applied in two places.

  • While elaborating. An array expression is a delayed value: a function from index to element; and the vertical fusion rules fire at the moment an operator is applied to one. F ∘ G below means "the element function of the result is F applied to the element function of the argument"; no pass looks for the pattern afterwards.
  • In the middle end. Elaboration produces the original compiler's indexified level: operator statements (IndexMap, IndexReduce, IndexScan, IndexFilter, and IndexScatter) over index spaces with ordinary scalar bodies (Specialization.operators prints it). Middle-end passes rewrite those statements in order: dead code elimination, normalization, vertical fusion (exact and affine map/scan/filter/reduce/scatter), filter fusion, sibling and online monoidal fusion, bilinear contraction reassociation, monoidal tiling and tile-interval pruning, chunkwise affine/bilinear scans, pairwise fold tiling, reduction interchange, and cache/register/GPU tiling. A final pass (LowerAdverbs in spirit) lowers operators into loops. parakeet.transforms.pipeline.PASSES is the authoritative list, and find_broken_transform toggles its passes on one at a time. See Algebraic laws for the mathematical identities behind these passes and the Kernel gallery for runnable examples.
map i_27, i_28 over (x_n0_3, y_n0_8):               # x @ y.T, as the passes see it
    off_29: int64 = (x_off_2 + (i_27 * x_n1_4))
    off_30: int64 = (y_off_7 + (i_28 * y_n1_9))
    reduce i_35 over (x_n1_4):
